22.title: Numbering Our Days: The Rhythm of Time at Home

mem.t: So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.

date.t: Giving Our Time a Seat at the Table
s: Get out your phones or a calendar together and look back over the past month. Count how many stretches of time belonged “just to the two of us.”
Each write down three things you “definitely want to do together next month.” Swap lists, pick two, and put them on the calendar first.
Agree on where your daily fifteen minutes will go from now on, and read Psalm 90:12 together.
Hold hands and pray: “Lord, our days are in your hands. Please teach us to number them.”

lessons.title: Counting Our Days
lessons.theme: Time is limited, which is why it is a treasure God entrusts to us

v: The days of our years are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty years; yet their pride is but labor and sorrow, for it passes quickly, and we fly away.
Who knows the power of your anger, your wrath according to the fear that is due to you?
So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.

lessons.still: Grow quiet and notice your breathing. Every breath in and every breath out is a free gift from God today. Whisper to the Lord: “Lord, my days are in your hands. Today, please teach me to treasure the time you have given us.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: People with self on the throne think time is “mine,” so my work, my hobbies and my phone come first. Self-emptied people admit that time belongs to God. They are willing to let Jesus reign and let him set the order of even their calendar: God → self → others → tasks.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. The night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9:4). He knew clearly that his time on earth was limited, yet he was never in a hurry, because every one of his days was lived according to his Father’s heart.
lessons.pray: Eternal Lord, our days are all in your hands. We confess that we often treat time as our own and get so busy that we forget you, and forget each other. Teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom, giving our best time to you and saving it for each other. Amen.
teach: Picture an hourglass sitting on your kitchen table. The sand keeps trickling down, never making a sound, never stopping. We often assume we have plenty of time: once work settles down, once the kids are older, once the mortgage is smaller, then we will really invest in our marriage. But the hourglass does not wait for us to be ready. Children grow up, parents grow old, and we ourselves move day by day into the second half of life.

Psalm 90 is a prayer of Moses. He saw that a human life “passes quickly, and we fly away” (Psalm 90:10). This is not pessimism; it is clear-eyed honesty. Then Moses asks God, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). Counting our days is not an anxious countdown. It is admitting that time is limited, and so it must be spent on what matters most.

Time is entrusted to us by God; it is not something we own. And whatever is entrusted brings a steward’s responsibility. When a couple counts their days together, they are asking together: How much of our time today went to God? How much did we save for each other? A marriage is like a garden. It does not need an occasional big project so much as daily watering. A heart of wisdom begins with seeing how precious time is.
q: If I look at our marriage as an hourglass, what conditions have I been waiting for before I really invest in it?
Which part of my time do I most often treat as “mine” rather than handing it over to God?
talk: If we had only one year left together, what are the three things you would most want to do with me?
In the past week, when did you most feel that I “had time” for you?
acts: Work out how many days you have been married and tell your spouse the number
Cut one unnecessary thing from today and give that time to your spouse
Before bed, pray over tomorrow’s time: “Lord, please set the order.”
lessons.noon: “So teach us to count our days” — Lord, right now I place the rest of today in your hands.

lessons.title: Redeeming the Time
lessons.theme: Making the most of our time means buying back the time that has been stolen

v: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise,
redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Therefore, don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.

lessons.still: Quietly think back over yesterday: from morning to night, where did your time go? No need to beat yourself up. Simply lay the day open honestly before the Lord and tell him, “Lord, please help me see it clearly.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Many couples have not stopped loving each other; they have simply let “tasks” steal the time meant for “people.” Redeeming the time means living out this order even on our calendar: never let tasks push aside the person beside us, our most important “2.”
lessons.jesus: Nicodemus “came to Jesus by night” (John 3:2). After a full day of ministry Jesus must have been tired, yet he did not send him away. He gave his evening to this one man and talked with him at length about being born again. Jesus shows us that love is willing to give precious time to a person.
lessons.pray: Lord, please forgive us for letting so many things steal our time with each other. Give us a heart of wisdom to understand your will and to know when to say “yes” and when to say “no.” Help us buy back our time and spend it on what you count most precious, and on each other. Amen.
teach: Paul writes about “redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:16). To redeem means to buy back, like hurrying to purchase something precious in the marketplace before someone else snaps it up. Time does not automatically get set aside for our marriage. If we do not deliberately buy it back, something else will buy it first.

Who is grabbing our time? Sometimes it is work, filling up the evenings after we get home. Sometimes it is the phone: one scroll, and an hour is gone. Sometimes it is busyness that looks spiritual, a church calendar so full that we never really look at our spouse. These things are not necessarily bad, but when they steal a couple’s time together, they become thieves in the marriage.

Paul goes on: “don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is” (Ephesians 5:17). Redeeming the time does not mean cramming our schedule even fuller. It means first understanding the Lord’s heart, then deciding what to say “yes” to and what to say “no” to. For a married couple, the Lord’s will is clear: he wants us to love each other and to build a household that belongs to God. For that purpose, our time is worth buying back.
q: What “thief” most often steals our time as a couple? Am I letting it get away with it?
Is there something I keep saying “yes” to that God actually wants me to learn to say “no” to?
talk: What do you think is the biggest “time thief” in our home? How could we buy that time back together?
Is there a time slot you would really love me to keep for you regularly?
acts: Check your phone’s screen-time report and share it honestly with your spouse
Choose one stretch of time tonight and leave your phone in another room
Gently say “Not this time” to one unnecessary invitation
lessons.noon: “redeeming the time, because the days are evil” — Lord, help me buy back this afternoon and spend it on what you count precious.

lessons.title: The Seasons and Rhythms of Marriage
lessons.theme: Marriage has seasons, and it also needs a steady rhythm

v: While the earth remains, seed time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night will not cease.”
He appointed the moon for seasons. The sun knows when to set.

lessons.still: Think about what season your marriage is in right now: the springtime of newlyweds, the full summer of raising children, a busy autumn harvest, or a quiet winter? Bring this season before the Lord and tell him, “Lord, this season, too, is in your hands.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When we complain that “this season is just too busy,” our focus is usually on our circumstances. To return to our rightful place is to admit that God rules the seasons and that my job within them is to be faithful. With our focus on Jesus rather than on our circumstances, we can build God’s rhythm in any season.
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ brothers urged him to go up to Jerusalem and make a name for himself, but Jesus said, “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready” (John 7:6). Jesus was not pushed along by other people’s timetables. He acted according to his Father’s timing, so he was never flustered.
lessons.pray: Lord who created the seasons, thank you for leading us through every season of our marriage. Whether this one is busy or quiet, help us accept it and build your rhythm within it. Teach us to put the big rocks into our life first, so the small stuff does not crowd out each other. Amen.
teach: After the flood, God promised: “While the earth remains, seed time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night will not cease” (Genesis 8:22). God designed a world with rhythm: sowing and reaping, cold and heat, day and night, round after round. Marriage has seasons too. As newlyweds we can talk endlessly; while raising children we can barely get enough sleep; in midlife we are stretched between work and aging parents; with an empty nest we must learn all over again how to be just the two of us. Couples without children also pass through different seasons of career, health and ministry.

Seasons change, but rhythm can stay steady. Imagine an empty glass jar. If you pour in the sand and pebbles first, the big rocks will not fit. If you put the big rocks in first, the sand fills in the gaps. A regular weekly time together as a couple is that big rock. It does not need to be expensive. It can be a walk or a quiet dinner. But it has to go on the calendar first, not wait until we “have time.”

The psalmist says, “He appointed the moon for seasons. The sun knows when to set” (Psalm 104:19). The sun and moon follow God’s arrangement, unhurried and never absent. A couple’s rhythm is the same. It is not a rigid rule but a fence that protects the relationship. In a busy season the rhythm can be shorter, but do not let it stop. In a more spacious season it can be longer, so you can really enjoy each other. Without deliberate planning, our moments together tend to just slip away.
q: What season is our marriage in right now? Am I accepting it, or have I been fighting it?
In my week, what is the “sand,” and what are the “big rocks”?
talk: In this season of ours, what do you think most needs protecting?
What time each week can we regularly keep for each other? Decide together on the exact day and time.
acts: Mark this week’s couple time on the calendar and keep it like a date
Write down one thing that is “sand” and can wait
Tell your spouse, “This time is for you, and I will guard it.”
lessons.noon: “seed time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night will not cease” — Lord, right now I trust that every season of our home is in your hands.

lessons.title: Fifteen Minutes a Day
lessons.theme: Small morning and evening rhythms add up to a lifetime of walking together

v: It is a good thing to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praises to your name, Most High,
to proclaim your loving kindness in the morning, and your faithfulness every night,
LORD, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.

lessons.still: Picture the first light of dawn coming through the window. In this moment, at the start or the end of your day, say to the Lord: “Lord, I come to you first. I want my first words and my last words today to be to you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Living from the head by ourselves, we keep waiting for “a big block of time” before we work on our marriage. Living from the heart by the Spirit, we start with today’s fifteen minutes. Change your mindset and your living will change; small rhythms are the very tracks that life change runs on.
lessons.jesus: As word about Jesus spread, great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed, “But he withdrew himself into the desert and prayed” (Luke 5:16). The bigger the crowds and the busier the days, the more he guarded his rhythm of time with the Father. That rhythm was the source of strength for all his ministry.
lessons.pray: Loving and faithful Lord, we want to proclaim your loving kindness in the morning and your faithfulness every night. Help us guard our fifteen minutes a day and not let busyness steal them. May our mornings begin with you and our nights rest in you, so that day by day we walk with you, and with each other. Amen.
teach: The psalmist says, “It is a good thing... to proclaim your loving kindness in the morning, and your faithfulness every night” (Psalm 92:1–2). Morning and evening are the two doorframes of the day. The Israelites offered sacrifices every morning and evening; Daniel prayed three times a day. Both used a steady rhythm to hand the day over to God. Spiritual strength rarely comes from one big breakthrough. It usually comes from small daily rhythms.

This app asks couples to spend fifteen minutes a day: five minutes alone with God, and ten minutes talking and praying together. Fifteen minutes sounds like very little, but it is like dropping a few coins into a piggy bank every day. Open it after a year and you will be amazed how heavy it has become. Even doing it only Monday to Friday adds up to more than sixty hours a year given entirely to God and to each other.

“In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly” (Psalm 5:3). Couples can have their own morning and evening doorframes too: a hug before leaving the house in the morning and an “I’m praying for you today”; at night before bed, the question “What wore you out most today?” These little rhythms do not need to be long, yet every day they bring two people back before God, and back to each other’s side.
q: Who usually gets my first thought and my last thought of the day?
Over these past few months, what excuse have I used most often to skip our daily fifteen minutes?
talk: What time of day is most realistic for our fifteen minutes: morning, midday, or bedtime?
As we leave in the morning or go to sleep at night, what is the one sentence you would most like to hear from me?
acts: Agree with your spouse on a set time for tomorrow’s fifteen minutes
Tomorrow morning before you leave, give your spouse a hug and a word of blessing
Before bed, ask your spouse: “What wore you out most today?”
lessons.noon: “to proclaim your loving kindness in the morning, and your faithfulness every night” — Lord, right here in the middle of my day, I remember your loving kindness again.

lessons.title: A Yearly Look Back: Setting Up Memorial Stones
lessons.theme: Only when we stop to remember do we see how God has helped us all along

v: that this may be a sign among you, that when your children ask in the future, saying, ‘What do you mean by these stones?’

then you shall tell them, ‘Because the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the LORD’s covenant. When it crossed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. These stones shall be for a memorial to the children of Israel forever.’”

You shall remember all the way which the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to test you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.

lessons.still: Think back over the road you have traveled since your wedding, with its mountaintops and valleys. Quietly let the Holy Spirit remind you of one thing God has brought you through, and say to the Lord: “Lord, thank you. All along the way, you have been the one guiding us.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When people with self on the throne look back, they remember only their own grievances and what the other person owes them. When self-emptied people look back, they see God’s grace first. Trade a human point of view for God’s point of view, and the very same year changes from “a hard year” into “a year we were helped.”
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, and said, “Do this in memory of me” (Luke 22:19). Jesus himself set up a rhythm of remembrance for his disciples, because he knew that grace remembered is grace that becomes the foundation of a life.
lessons.pray: Lord who has guided us all along the way, thank you for leading our marriage through the easy times and through the wilderness. We often forget your grace and remember only the hardships. Open our eyes to see your hand in every season. Help us set up memorial stones, so that our family will tell of your faithfulness for generations. Amen.
teach: After the Israelites crossed the Jordan, God told them to take twelve stones from the riverbed and pile them up at Gilgal. Why? So that “when your children ask in the future, saying, ‘What do you mean by these stones?’” (Joshua 4:6), they could tell of what God had done. We forget so easily, and so God teaches us to set up stones of remembrance.

After forty years in the wilderness Moses told the people, “You shall remember all the way which the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness” (Deuteronomy 8:2). God wanted Israel to remember not only the victories of entering Canaan but also the wilderness years: manna in their lack, guidance in their trials. Looking back does not mean remembering only the good parts. It means seeing God’s hand in both the easy times and the hard times.

Couples need a yearly “memorial stone” too. It could be on your wedding anniversary, or at the end or start of the year: stop together and look back. Three questions are enough: What has God done in our home this year? What are we most thankful for? Where do we want to go together next year? Write down your answers, and they become your family’s memorial stones. Our days become meaningful as we count them, and our marriage grows stronger as we remember.
q: What is one thing God did in our home this past year that I almost forgot to thank him for?
When I look back, do my grievances come to mind first, or God’s grace?
talk: If we set up a memorial stone for our marriage, what one event would you carve on it?
What day would we like to set aside each year to look back together?
acts: Write down three things God did in your home this year
Choose a date to be your yearly couple’s look-back day
Tell your spouse, in one sentence, one thing you are thankful for
lessons.noon: “You shall remember all the way which the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness” — Lord, right now I remember how you have guided me all along the way.

23.title: Rest and Presence: Put Down the Phone, See Each Other

mem.t: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.

s: Before you head out, put both phones together in a box or drawer and agree not to look at them for the next two hours (you can keep one on hand for family emergencies).
Go somewhere quiet for a walk or a cup of tea, and take turns saying: “This week, the one thing I most want you to know is…”
Look your spouse in the eyes and name one thing about them that you noticed afresh today.
Before going home, read Matthew 11:28 together and pray for each other, asking the Lord to give you true rest.

lessons.title: Rest Is God’s Gift
lessons.theme: God rested first, and he invites us to stop too

v: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
He said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.

lessons.still: Right now, let yourself truly stop. Set aside what is in your hands, let your shoulders drop, and say to the Lord: “Lord, the world does not run on me; you hold all things together. I can rest in you for a while.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Sometimes we cannot stop because of self on the throne: we feel things will fall apart without us, as if we were the center of the world. Rest is a way to return to our rightful place: let people be people, and let God be God. Only when we admit our limits can we experience God’s limitlessness.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus’ disciples picked heads of grain on the Sabbath, the Pharisees criticized them. Jesus did not weigh them down with more rules. Instead he explained what the Sabbath was really for. He cared about people’s needs, and he showed that the heart of rest is not rules but a heart in fellowship with God.
lessons.pray: Lord, Creator of all things, thank you for giving us a rhythm of rest. We confess that we often cannot stop, as if everything depended on us. Teach us to stop and rest in you, and to place our home in your hands. May our rest become a declaration of faith, and a space for loving each other. Amen.
teach: When God had finished his work of creation, “he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done” (Genesis 2:2). The almighty God was not tired. He was setting a rhythm for the world he had made: after work, stop to admire, to enjoy, to give thanks. And “God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy” (Genesis 2:3). Rest is not wasted time. It is time blessed by God and set apart as holy.

Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). Rest is God’s gift to us, not a burden laid on us. Just as a phone needs recharging, people need to stop. Many couples have not stopped wanting to love each other; they are simply too tired: too tired to talk, so tired that the smallest thing sets off a flash of temper. It is hard for exhausted people to be gentle.

The Sabbath principle reminds us that stopping is an act of faith. When we put down our work, we are declaring: “It is God who provides for this family, not my endless striving.” Couples can recover a weekly rhythm of rest together: a stretch of time with no talk of work, no household chores, no rush to get anything done, simply worshiping God, resting, and enjoying each other.
q: What makes it hardest for me to stop: a sense of duty, insecurity, or the feeling that I am indispensable?
When was the last time I truly “rested,” rather than just “zoning out”?
talk: How many bars do you think our family’s “battery” has left lately? What drains you most?
If we had half a day each week as our own time of rest, how would you most like to spend it?
acts: Tonight give yourself ten minutes to do nothing but be quiet before the Lord
Talk with your spouse about which half-day this week could be your time of rest
Tell your spouse: “You’ve worked so hard. Get to bed early tonight.”
lessons.noon: “The Sabbath was made for man” — Lord, I pause right now and acknowledge that you are the one who holds everything together.

lessons.title: Come to Jesus and Find Rest
lessons.theme: Only when we find rest in Jesus can we bring rest to our home

v: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

lessons.still: Imagine you have been walking a long way carrying a heavy backpack. Now Jesus stands in front of you, holds out his hand, and says, “Give it to me.” Quietly tell him about the heaviest thing on your heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus says, “learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). Proud people carry everything themselves and demand that others carry things their way too; humble people hand their burdens to the Lord. Jesus is my example, and humility is where true rest is found.
lessons.jesus: The disciples were so busy they did not even have time to eat. Jesus said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile” (Mark 6:31). Jesus saw how worn out they were and personally took them away to rest. He does not only send people out to work; he also leads them into rest.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, gentle and humble in heart, we come to you with our own burdens. Free us from the weariness of carrying everything alone, and let us find rest in you. Help us, when we come home, not to turn our burdens into pressure on each other, but to hand them over to you together. Amen.
teach: Jesus said, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Jesus did not say, “Sort out your burdens first, then come.” We can come with our burdens still on our backs. Many couples carry heavy loads in their marriage: financial pressure, problems with the children, caring for aging parents, disappointment in each other. If these burdens just get passed back and forth between the two of them, in the end both will be crushed.

Jesus goes on: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me” (Matthew 11:29). A yoke is a wooden frame fitted over the necks of two oxen so they can pull the plow side by side. It is a beautiful picture of marriage: husband and wife sharing one yoke, shoulder to shoulder. But even more important, Jesus invites us to share a yoke with him. When Jesus is on the other side of the yoke, he carries the heaviest end.

Jesus says, “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). Not because life has become simpler, but because we no longer carry it alone. Someone who has found rest in Jesus does not come home and dump the whole day’s exhaustion and anger on their spouse. Only when we are with God can we truly be with others; when there is rest in our hearts, there will be rest in our home.
q: What is the heaviest burden I am carrying right now? Have I been carrying it only in my own heart instead of handing it to Jesus?
Do I often end up unloading my exhaustion and stress onto my spouse without realizing it?
talk: What burden have you been carrying lately that I don’t really know about yet? How can I help you hand it to the Lord together?
When do you feel that we are “sharing one yoke,” rather than each pulling our own way?
acts: Write down one burden, pray over it, and hand it to the Lord
Before you walk in the door at home, pause, take a deep breath, and pray one sentence in your heart
Ask your spouse: “Is there anything I can take off your plate today?”
lessons.noon: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” — Lord Jesus, right now I lay this burden under your yoke.

lessons.title: Living Together Is Not the Same as Being Together
lessons.theme: Under the same roof, and also of one heart

v: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.still: Think back to how the two of you were at home last night. You were in the same space, but what was each of you doing? No need to blame yourself. Simply say to the Lord: “Lord, please teach me what it means to be truly present.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Hidden inside Martha’s distraction was a “self”: I’ve done so much, why doesn’t anyone care? Service with self on the throne easily turns into complaining. Self-emptied people choose first to be with the Lord, and then their service flows out of rest instead of being squeezed out of busyness.
lessons.jesus: A rich young man came to ask about eternal life, and “Jesus looking at him loved him” (Mark 10:21). Before saying a word of teaching, Jesus first looked at this man with full attention. His presence was not distracted company but wholehearted attention.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, like Martha we are often anxious and troubled about many things. Teach us to choose the good part and to sit at your feet first. Help us at home not just to live together but to be truly present to each other, with our eyes on each other and our hearts turned toward each other. Amen.
teach: Picture an evening: the husband on the couch looking at his phone, the wife in bed looking at hers, the kids in their room playing video games. The whole family is home, yet each is living on a separate island. This is “living together without being together”: bodies in the same place, hearts somewhere else. Sometimes the greatest danger to a marriage is not fighting but slowly drifting into separate lives.

Martha eagerly welcomed Jesus, but “Martha was distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40). Everything she did was good, yet in her distraction she complained, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone?” (Luke 10:40). Mary, meanwhile, “sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word” (Luke 10:39). Jesus said, “one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part” (Luke 10:42).

It was not that Martha did not love Jesus. She was just so busy that she forgot to be with him. Couples do the same: busy for the household, busy for the kids, busy making a living, and forgetting to sit down and really look at each other. Being present matters more than sharing an address. First sit at Jesus’ feet like Mary, then learn to sit beside your spouse, put down what is in your hands, and listen with your full attention.
q: At home, am I more like Martha or Mary? What expectations are hidden behind my busyness?
Lately, have I been doing other things while my spouse was talking to me?
talk: When do you most feel that I am “here in body and in heart”? What am I doing at those times?
Which part of our evening could we agree to set aside, putting everything down just to sit together and talk?
acts: Tonight, when you talk with your spouse, put everything down and look at them
Find a time for the two of you to sit together for ten minutes without doing anything
Write down one thing that has you “distracted,” and give it to the Lord
lessons.noon: “one thing is needed” — Lord, right now I put down my busyness and choose to be with you.

lessons.title: Put Down the Phone, See Each Other
lessons.theme: Only when we put down the screen in our hands can we see the person in front of us

v: “Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted in the earth.”
My dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding places of the mountainside, let me see your face. Let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet and your face is lovely.

lessons.still: Move your phone a little further away, or turn it face down. Notice the empty feeling of not having it in your hand. Say to the Lord: “Lord, please fill my heart, so my hands are free to hold the people I love.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Cutting back on the phone is not just changing a habit; it is changing our mindset: who is reigning? If I drop my spouse the moment my phone buzzes, the screen has taken the throne in my heart. To let Jesus reign is to give our attention first to God, and then to the person in front of us.
lessons.jesus: In the synagogue there was a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years and could not straighten up. “When Jesus saw her, he called her” (Luke 13:12). Everyone was listening to the teaching, but Jesus’ eyes saw this person in the corner. His attention was never carried off by the crowd; he always saw the one.
lessons.pray: Lord, we want to be still and know that you are God. Forgive us for so often letting screens steal our attention from each other. Help us put down our phones and see the person you have given us, to see their face and hear their voice. May our eyes look first to you, and then turn tenderly toward each other. Amen.
teach: God says, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). The Hebrew word behind “be still” carries the sense of letting go, of stopping, like a clenched hand opening. For many people today, the hardest thing to let go of is the phone. It brings convenience, but it also quietly steals our attention: we look at it during meals, before sleep, and first thing when we wake up. The phone itself is not sin, but when it keeps us from seeing our spouse, it becomes a third party in our marriage.

In the Song of Songs the lover says to his beloved: “let me see your face. Let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet and your face is lovely” (Song of Songs 2:14). This is the deepest longing of people in love: to be seen and to be heard. But if our eyes are always fixed on a screen, we will not see the tiredness on our spouse’s face, or hear the hurt in their voice.

Couples can set phone-free times for the household together: for example at meals, during our daily fifteen minutes, and for the half hour before bed, putting phones in a set basket. This is not about policing each other but about protecting each other’s attention together. It may feel strange at first, but gradually we discover that once the phone is down, we see again that familiar, lovable face.
q: How does the time I spend on my phone each day compare with the time I spend giving my spouse my full attention?
At what moments does my phone most often “carry me away” from my spouse?
talk: Which of my phone habits makes you feel most ignored? Please tell me gently; I want to change.
What two phone-free times could our household set together? How can we gently remind each other?
acts: At dinner tonight, put both your phones in the same basket
Turn off one unnecessary notification
Look into your spouse’s eyes and listen until they finish telling you something
lessons.noon: “Be still, and know that I am God” — Lord, right now I put down the screen in my hand and look to you first.

lessons.title: With God First, Then with Each Other
lessons.theme: God’s presence is the source of rest in our home

v: He said, “My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.”
Moses said to him, “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here.

lessons.still: Think back over this week. When did you most sense God’s presence? And when did he seem far away? Quietly say to the Lord: “Lord, if your presence doesn’t go with me, I don’t want to go.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. If we are not first with God, we will try to get from our spouse the rest that only God can give, and we end up making demands on each other and disappointing each other. With our focus on Jesus, our spouse moves from the role of “provider” back to the role of “companion.”
lessons.jesus: When Jesus chose the twelve disciples, his first purpose was “that they might be with him” (Mark 3:14), and only then would he send them out to preach. Jesus shows us that presence comes before work. When we are first with the Lord, our lives have strength to love and to serve.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, we do not want a life without your presence. Please go with us yourself and give our home rest. Help us first to be still before you, and then to become rest for each other at home. May every day and every week of ours have the rhythm of your presence. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
teach: After the Israelites worshiped the golden calf, God said he would no longer go with them himself. When Moses heard this, he pleaded earnestly. God answered, “My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest” (Exodus 33:14). Moses said, “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here” (Exodus 33:15). Moses would rather not enter the good land of Canaan than have a future without God’s presence.

This tells us that true rest does not come from smooth circumstances, but from God’s presence. A family can have a nice house, a good income and good schools, yet without God’s presence it will still find no rest. A family can go through storms, yet with God’s presence there is rest. The source of rest in a home is not how much we do but whether God goes with us.

This week we have talked about rest, presence, and putting down our phones. The foundation of all of it is being with God first, and then with each other. Just as a lamp must be plugged in before it can shine, we must first find rest before God before we can become rest for each other at home. Together you could design a “rest rhythm” for your home: the daily fifteen minutes, weekly phone-free times, and half a day each week for rest and worship.
q: Do I expect my spouse to give me rest and satisfaction that only God can give?
What is the one “rest rhythm” from this week that I most want to keep?
talk: From this week’s lessons, what would you most like us to start doing at home?
Let’s design a rest rhythm for our home together: what will we guard each day, and each week?
acts: Write down your home’s “rest rhythm” with your spouse and stick it on the fridge
Make the first thing you do today praying to God, before picking up your phone
Tell your spouse: “Having you beside me makes me feel safe.”
lessons.noon: “My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest” — Lord, right now please be with me yourself and give me rest.

24.title: Walking Together: Dates and Adventures as a Couple

mem.t: Live joyfully with the wife whom you love all the days of your life of vanity, which he has given you under the sun, all your days of vanity, for that is your portion in life, and in your labor in which you labor under the sun.

s: Go back to where you had your first date, or a place you often went when you first met. If you can’t get there, set up a similar corner at home.
Take turns saying: “Back then, what attracted me most to you was…; now, what I appreciate even more about you is…”
Do something fun together that will make you laugh, like baking a dessert, playing a game, or racing to see who can spot a certain thing first on a walk.
Before heading home, read Ecclesiastes 9:9 together and thank God for giving you to each other as lifelong companions.

lessons.title: Can Two Walk Together?
lessons.theme: Walking together takes agreement, and agreement takes setting a time to meet

v: Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?

lessons.still: Picture the two of you walking side by side down a little path, sometimes faster, sometimes slower. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, lately have we been walking side by side, or one ahead and one behind, each going our own way?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Disagreement usually grows from self on the throne: I want to go my way and I expect you to keep up. Only the self-emptied life makes oneness possible. When both are willing to let Jesus reign, we share a direction. It is not you following me, or me following you, but both of us following the Lord together.
lessons.jesus: During his three years on earth, Jesus often walked with his disciples, ate with them, and went up mountains and out on the lake with them. He did not only teach them in gatherings; he kept them company along the road. Jesus shows us that relationships are built on the road we walk together.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that we can walk together on the road of life. Make us of one heart, not just living under one roof but walking side by side. Help us deliberately set aside time, pause regularly to check our direction, and walk toward you together. Amen.
teach: The prophet Amos asks, “Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?” (Amos 3:3). The word “agreed” here carries the sense of making an appointment, arranging to meet. If two people are going to walk together, they first have to agree on a time, a place and a direction. Without that, even living in the same city, they will hardly ever end up walking together.

This is exactly what dating as a married couple is about. Many couples dated often before the wedding, but afterward they feel, “We live together now, why bother making dates?” Yet living together is not the same as walking together. Without deliberate plans, two people are easily pushed in different directions by work, children and errands, until one day they look up and realize how far apart they have drifted. A date is a regular way of agreeing again: we are still walking together.

Being in agreement does not mean two people think exactly the same; it means they are heading the same way: toward God, and toward each other. It is like two people rowing the same boat. Their strength and rhythm are different, but as long as they row in the same direction, the boat moves forward. A date is not just dinner and a movie. It is pausing in the busyness to make sure we are still heading in the same direction.
q: When was the last time we “made a date” for time that belonged just to the two of us?
When it comes to the direction of our marriage, do I often expect my spouse to keep up with me, instead of both of us following the Lord?
talk: If our marriage were a rowboat, do you feel we’ve been rowing in the same direction lately, or each rowing our own way?
How often, and when, can we schedule a regular date? Let’s decide on the details together.
acts: Set up a date of at least thirty minutes with your spouse this week
After work or after dinner today, take a ten-minute walk together
Ask your spouse: “This year, where would you most like us to go together?”
lessons.noon: “Do two walk together, unless they have agreed” — Lord, right now please make us of one heart as we follow you together.

lessons.title: The Blessing of Living Joyfully
lessons.theme: Enjoying our spouse is a portion God gives us, not a waste

v: Go your way—eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works.
Let your garments be always white, and don’t let your head lack oil.

Live joyfully with the wife whom you love all the days of your life of vanity, which he has given you under the sun, all your days of vanity, for that is your portion in life, and in your labor in which you labor under the sun.

lessons.still: Let the muscles of your face relax; maybe even smile a little. Remember that God is a God of joy. Tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you that we don’t only suffer together; we also get to be happy together.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Seen in the light of eternity, life really is short, and precisely because it is short, we should treasure the person God has given us. From a human point of view a date is an expense; from God’s point of view it is faithful stewardship: taking good care of the marriage he has entrusted to me.
lessons.jesus: Jesus ate with people so often that he was criticized for it: “The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Behold, a glutton and a drunkard’” (Luke 7:34). Jesus was not a gloomy ascetic. He enjoyed the joy of sharing a table with people, and he brought God’s Kingdom to every table.
lessons.pray: Lord of all grace, thank you for giving us to each other as our portion in all our labor under the sun. Forgive us for treating our spouse as a responsibility instead of a gift. Help us, even in busy times, to know how to rejoice together and enjoy the good things you give. Amen.
teach: Ecclesiastes often says “vanity,” yet in the middle of all that vanity it offers a warm piece of advice: “Live joyfully with the wife whom you love all the days of your life of vanity... for that is your portion in life, and in your labor in which you labor under the sun” (Ecclesiastes 9:9). Though these words are addressed to husbands, they apply just as much to wives. In a life of hard work, our spouse is the portion God gives us, a gift and not a burden.

The Teacher also says, “Go your way—eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works” (Ecclesiastes 9:7). Some Christians feel that enjoyment is unspiritual, as if the harder life is, the more godly we are. But Scripture says that enjoying the good things God gives, rejoicing together with our spouse in thankfulness, is pleasing to God. A date is not a waste of time and money; it is an investment in a relationship God has given.

Imagine a car that is driven constantly but never refueled or serviced. Sooner or later it ends up stalled by the side of the road. Dates are a marriage’s filling station. They don’t have to be expensive: a cup of coffee, a picnic in the park, an old movie together, any of these will do. What matters is that during this time you don’t talk about bills or the kids’ problems; you simply enjoy each other’s company.
q: Deep down, do I feel that “enjoying ourselves” is unspiritual, or that dates are a waste?
When was the last time I simply enjoyed being with my spouse, rather than handling things together?
talk: For you, what does a “recharging” date look like? It doesn’t have to cost much.
On our next date, which topics can we agree not to bring up, so we can both really rest?
acts: Tell your spouse today: “Thank God for giving you to me.”
List three inexpensive date ideas you would both enjoy
Share a small treat with your spouse tonight and have a good ten-minute chat
lessons.noon: “Live joyfully with the wife whom you love” — Lord, right now I thank you for giving me a companion for life.

lessons.title: Being Each Other’s Best Friend
lessons.theme: The best spouses are also the best of friends

v: His mouth is sweetness; yes, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.
A man of many companions may be ruined, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.

lessons.still: Think of the best friend you have ever had, and the ease and trust you felt with them. Now think of your spouse. Say to the Lord: “Lord, please make us each other’s best friend.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: My spouse is my most important “2,” my spiritual companion and my lifelong friend. People with self on the throne just want their spouse to meet their needs; self-emptied people are willing to step into the other person’s world and become curious about what they love. That is where friendship begins.
lessons.jesus: Scripture says, “Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus” (John 11:5). Jesus often stayed at their home in Bethany, eating, resting, and talking heart to heart. Later he said, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep” (John 11:11). The Lord of all things also treasured friendship in the ordinary life of a home.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for calling us your friends. Make us not only husband and wife but each other’s best friend. Help us stay curious about each other’s world, be willing to share our hearts, and enjoy life together. Let our marriage take root in friendship and grow closer as we go. Amen.
teach: In the Song of Songs, the bride says of her beloved: “This is my beloved, and this is my friend” (Song of Songs 5:16). She does not only say “this is my lover”; she also says “this is my friend.” Romance makes the heart race; friendship lets the heart rest. The feelings of being in love rise and fall, but a deep friendship lets a marriage go the distance.

Proverbs says, “there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24). In marriage, our spouse can become that kind of friend. What marks a friend? Enjoying being together, being able to speak from the heart, sharing interests, appreciating each other, and sticking by each other in hard times. Many couples, after years of marriage, have become excellent “work partners,” handling chores, kids and bills together, but have gradually stopped being friends.

To rekindle friendship, start with small things: become curious again about each other’s world. Ask what your spouse has been thinking about, reading, or worrying about lately. Build a shared interest, like walking, gardening, cooking, or reading a book together. Remember the little things they love. Friendship is like a potted plant: it doesn’t need a flood of water every day, but it can’t be forgotten for long.
q: Right now, are we more like friends, or more like partners who handle tasks together?
What has my spouse been caring about, worrying over, or enjoying lately? Do I really know?
talk: If we were to build a shared interest, what would you most like us to do together?
When do you feel I am most like your “best friend”? What was I doing then?
acts: Ask your spouse a question you have never asked before
Decide together on one shared interest to build
Send your spouse a message today telling them they are your best friend
lessons.noon: “there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother” — Lord, right now I thank you that my spouse is also my friend.

lessons.title: Laughing Together: Rekindling the Fun
lessons.theme: A home filled with laughter testifies that God has done great things

v: When the LORD brought back those who returned to Zion, we were like those who dream.
Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing. Then they said among the nations, “The LORD has done great things for them.”
The LORD has done great things for us, and we are glad.

lessons.still: Recall the time you two laughed the hardest together, and let that picture linger in your heart. Thank the Lord for being with you in that moment. Say to him: “Lord, please let laughter return to our home.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Joy depends on the Lord, not on circumstances. People with self on the throne wait for circumstances to improve before they are happy, and wait for the other person to change before they are willing to play; self-emptied people bring joy home first. From a human point of view we “have no time for fun”; from God’s point of view, laughter is a way of counting the great things he has done.
lessons.jesus: Jesus noticed children playing games in the marketplace and used them in a parable: “We piped to you, and you didn’t dance” (Luke 7:32). He knew the joys and games of everyday life, and he grieved over people whose hearts were so hard they would not rejoice even when it was time to rejoice.
lessons.pray: Lord who does great things, what you have done for our home lets our mouths be filled with laughter. Bring joy back into our home, so that we are not only reminding and critiquing each other, but laughing and going on adventures together. Help us catch the little foxes that steal our joy, and enjoy the good things you have prepared. Amen.
teach: When the exiled Israelites returned to Zion, the psalmist said, “we were like those who dream,” and then, “Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing” (Psalm 126:2). God had done great things, and his people laughed out loud. Laughter is not frivolous; it is the natural response of people who have received grace. A home that often rings with laughter is itself a testimony: God has done great things here.

But the pressures of life often make couples far too serious: all our conversations are reminders, critiques and logistics, until home starts to feel like an office. Every now and then, letting our guard down together, playing a game, telling a joke, or doing something a bit silly, can soften a stiff relationship again. Getting away together works the same way: step out the door into a new setting, and often our mood changes too, and we see again how lovable the other person is.

The Song of Songs says, “Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that plunder the vineyards” (Song of Songs 2:15). The joy of marriage is often stolen by little foxes: being too busy, too tired, too petty, too worried about what others think. Couples can agree that on dates and outings they will leave these little foxes outside the door, remember together the great things God has done for their home, and have a good laugh.
q: Lately at home, have I been smiling more, or frowning more?
Which “little foxes” most often steal the fun between us?
talk: What is the most fun, most unforgettable thing we have ever done together?
Over the next month, where would you most like to go with me?
acts: Tell your spouse a joke or share something funny today
Plan a short trip together and put it on the calendar
Write down one “little fox” you want to catch
lessons.noon: “The LORD has done great things for us, and we are glad” — Lord, right now I count the great things you have done for our home.

lessons.title: A Couple Who Walks with God
lessons.theme: The highest goal of walking together is walking with God together

v: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does the LORD require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.

lessons.still: Picture the two of you walking down a road at dusk, sharing what is on your hearts. Now picture the Lord walking right between you. Quietly say to him: “Lord, we want not only to walk with each other, but to walk with you together.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Walking humbly is the key to walking with God. Proud people want God to follow them, and want their spouse to follow them too; humble people return to their rightful place and follow God. When we let Jesus reign, husband and wife no longer argue about who leads; we follow him together.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “If a man loves me, he will keep my word. My Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him” (John 14:23). What Jesus promises is not an occasional visit, but to make his home in our lives and in our households, walking and living with us every day.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you for being willing to make your home with us and walk with us. Teach us at home to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly. May we not only walk with each other but walk with you together, drawing closer to you, and to each other, step by step through ordinary days. Amen.
teach: Scripture’s record of Enoch is short, yet it stirs our longing: “Enoch walked with God” (Genesis 5:24). He was no hermit. The Bible tells us he had sons and daughters and lived an ordinary family life, yet he walked with God in daily life for three hundred years. Walking with God does not mean leaving family life behind; it means walking with God every day right in the middle of it.

The prophet Micah says that what God requires is “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). This is also the best guide for a couple walking together. To act justly is to be honest and fair at home. To love mercy is to show a little more understanding toward our spouse’s weaknesses. To walk humbly is to be willing to give way first and apologize first. When we live out all three at home, we are walking with God.

This week we have talked about making dates, enjoying each other, being friends, and laughing together. In the end, all our walking together must return to this center: the two of us walking with God together. It is like three people walking side by side: when the two on the outside both draw closer to the one in the middle, they naturally draw closer to each other. May our dates and adventures not only bring our hearts closer to each other, but bring both our hearts closer to the Lord.
q: In the everyday life of our home, what part looks most like “walking with God”? What part looks least like it?
Of justice, mercy and humility, which do I most need to practice at home?
talk: Of this week’s reminders, which would you most like us to put into practice in our marriage?
On our next date, how could we naturally “walk with God” together? For example, by giving thanks or praying together.
acts: On a walk with your spouse today, each share one thing you’re thankful for
At home, be the first to give way or the first to apologize about something
Write down the date and place of your next date
lessons.noon: “to walk humbly with your God” — Lord, right now I choose to walk humbly with you.

25.title: Everything Belongs to God: The Lordship of Money

mem.t: The earth is the LORD’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it.

s: Find a relaxed spot and each share: How did your family talk about money when you were growing up? How have your parents’ attitudes toward money shaped who you are today?
Take turns telling one specific time when “God provided for our family,” and thank each other.
Set a time next week to sit down together and look at your household income and spending. Today, just set the time; no need to rush into the numbers.
Read Psalm 24:1 together, then open your hands and pray: “Lord, everything we have is yours.”

lessons.title: The Earth and Its Fullness
lessons.theme: From “my money” to “God’s money”

v: The earth is the LORD’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it.
For he has founded it on the seas, and established it on the floods.
But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.

lessons.still: Open your hands, palms up. Think: what these hands have earned and what they hold, where did it come from? Quietly say to the Lord: “Lord, everything in my hands is yours.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: “This is my money” is the most common sentence of the self-ruled life. When the spouse who earns more wants to call the shots and the spouse who earns less feels they have no say, both have left their rightful place. When we return to our rightful place and acknowledge that God is the Owner, husband and wife are both stewards, equally honored before God.
lessons.jesus: Some people tried to trap Jesus with a question about taxes. Jesus held up a coin and asked, “Whose is this image and inscription?” Then he said, “Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21). The coin bore Caesar’s image, but we bear the image of God, so our whole selves belong to God.
lessons.pray: Lord of all, the earth and its fullness belong to you, and everything we have comes from you. We confess that we often treat money as our own, and even compete with each other over it. Change our mindset, and make us your faithful stewards together, using what you have entrusted to us with one heart before you. Amen.
teach: Imagine handing your car keys to a valet at a hotel entrance. He can drive the car, park it, and hold on to the keys, but he would never say, “This is my car.” He knows he is only entrusted with it. The psalmist says, “The earth is the LORD’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it” (Psalm 24:1). Our house, our income, our savings, even we ourselves, all belong to God. We are not owners; we are stewards.

King David gathered enormous resources to build the temple, and the people gave gladly too. Yet when David prayed, he said, “For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own” (1 Chronicles 29:14). David did not boast about how much he had donated; he acknowledged that everything had always belonged to God. This is where the Bible’s view of money begins: not “How much do I give God?” but “How much has God entrusted to me?”

Once this mindset changes, the way a couple talks about money changes too. If the money is “mine,” fights come easily: who earns more, who gets the final say, who is wasting it. If the money is “God’s,” husband and wife stand together before the Owner and ask the same question: Lord, how do you want us to use what you have entrusted to us? Money is no longer a tool of power but a trust we will give account for together before God.
q: In my heart, does our household money feel more like “my money,” “our money,” or “God’s money”?
Has how much I earn affected how much say I feel I have at home?
talk: How did each of our families of origin view money? How have those views shaped us today?
If we truly believed that “the money is God’s,” what do you think would change first in our home?
acts: Write “This is God’s” on your wallet or next to your phone’s payment screen
Thank God for your household income, naming one specific thing
Tell your spouse: “Let’s be God’s stewards together.”
lessons.noon: “The earth is the LORD’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it” — Lord, right now I acknowledge that everything in my hands is yours.

lessons.title: Where Your Treasure Is, There Your Heart Will Be
lessons.theme: Money is a touchstone that reveals who truly rules the heart

v: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal;
but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal;
for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.

lessons.still: Open your spending records for the past month, or simply think back over them. Don’t rush to judge; just quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, from the way I spend money, what do you see that my heart cares about most?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Never let things wreck a relationship. When we fight about money, “tasks” and “things” have usually jumped ahead of “people.” When Jesus reigns, money cannot reign. When the order of our relationships returns to God → self → others → tasks, money becomes a blessing rather than a temptation.
lessons.jesus: When a man asked Jesus to settle an inheritance, Jesus warned the crowd: “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses” (Luke 12:15). Jesus did not take sides in the property dispute; he went straight to the heart: the worth of a life does not lie in how much we own.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you see right through our hearts, and you see how we use money. Forgive us for the times we have let money become our master and let worry and comparison rob us of peace. We want to serve you alone. Turn our hearts toward heaven, and put money back in its place as a servant. Amen.
teach: Jesus said, “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). Many people think the heart decides where the money goes, but Jesus says that where the money goes, the heart follows. A bank statement is actually a very honest report on the soul: it records what we really care about.

Jesus goes on: “You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24). “Mammon” means wealth, and Jesus personifies it, as if it were a master demanding to be served. Money is a good servant but a bad master. When money becomes master, it leads us around by the nose: worrying there won’t be enough, fearing loss, comparing ourselves with others, until even our marriage is ruled by it.

Money is a touchstone for a marriage. Many couples’ arguments look like they are about money, but underneath they are about security, self-worth and control: one spouse saves because they fear running short, the other spends because they long to be affirmed. When together we lay up treasure in heaven, that is, when we put God first, money returns to its place as a servant, and husband and wife stop hurting each other over it.
q: If my spending record were a “report on my soul,” what would it show I care about most?
Behind my anxiety about money, or my craving for it, what am I afraid of, or what am I hoping to get?
talk: When we disagree about money, what is usually your deepest worry? Please tell me; I want to understand.
In what way do you think our family most looks like we are “laying up treasure in heaven”?
acts: Look at your biggest recent purchase and ask yourself what it reveals
Write down one money worry and hand it to the Lord
Tell your spouse one worry you have about money, not to get it fixed but just to be heard
lessons.noon: “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” — Lord, right now I set my heart on you once again.

lessons.title: In the Light: Financial Transparency as a Couple
lessons.theme: Financial transparency is the foundation of trust, not a way to monitor each other

v: We are avoiding this, that any man should blame us concerning this abundance which is administered by us.
Having regard for honorable things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.
He who walks blamelessly walks surely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out.

lessons.still: Quietly ask yourself: when it comes to money, is there anything I don’t want my spouse to know? Don’t be afraid. The Lord already knows, and he still loves you. Tell him: “Lord, I want to live in the light.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Hiding and controlling are both expressions of the self-ruled life: one wants to keep a private space, the other wants to hold on to power. Only the self-emptied life makes oneness possible. When both acknowledge that the money is God’s, are transparent before God, and are honest with each other, trust will slowly grow.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God” (John 3:21). Jesus’ whole life had nothing to hide, and he invites us to step out of the darkness and live in the light too. The light is not there to condemn us, but to bring healing and freedom.
lessons.pray: Lord of light, you search our hearts, and nothing can be hidden from you. Forgive us for hiding things and controlling each other with money. Give us courage to step into the light and be honest with each other; and give us gentle hearts, so that when the other opens up, we do not condemn but face it together. May our home grow strong in trust. Amen.
teach: When Paul collected an offering for the poor in Jerusalem, he deliberately had trustworthy brothers handle it with him. He wrote, “We are avoiding this, that any man should blame us concerning this abundance which is administered by us,” and added, “Having regard for honorable things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” (2 Corinthians 8:20–21). Even an apostle handling money made a point of keeping the accounts out in the light.

Between husband and wife, that kind of light is needed even more. Many families today have secrets: one spouse secretly borrows money or runs up a credit card, one keeps a private stash the other doesn’t know about, or one hides investment losses. Proverbs says, “he who perverts his ways will be found out” (Proverbs 10:9). A small cover-up is like a crack in a wall: hardly visible at first, but over time it can bring the whole wall down. Financial transparency means that both spouses know about income, savings, debts and major expenses, and decide about them together.

But we must be clear about one distinction: transparency is not surveillance, and stewardship is not control. If one spouse uses money to control the other, for example by keeping the other from knowing the household finances, taking the other’s income, restricting basic living needs, or using money to threaten or humiliate them, this is financial control and abuse. It is not submission, and it is not good stewardship. If this is happening to you, your safety comes first. Please seek help from a pastor you trust and from professional support services.
q: Is there anything about money, big or small, that I have kept from my spouse? How am I willing to bring it into the light?
Have I ever used money to show displeasure, to gain the upper hand, or in ways that made my spouse feel insecure?
talk: For you, what does financial “transparency” between us specifically include? Where could we start?

Above what amount do we want to talk with each other before spending? Agree together on a figure you both feel at peace with. If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down what you would like to say to them.
acts: If you have been hiding something financial, pray for courage today and set a time to tell your spouse
Schedule a family finance meeting with your spouse
Tell your spouse: “Whatever you tell me, I am willing to face it with you.”
lessons.noon: “He who walks blamelessly walks surely” — Lord, right now I choose to walk blamelessly in how I handle money.

lessons.title: Good and Faithful Stewards
lessons.theme: Managing every dollar well is faithfulness to God

v: “Now after a long time the lord of those servants came, and settled accounts with them.
He who received the five talents came and brought another five talents, saying, ‘Lord, you delivered to me five talents. Behold, I have gained another five talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
Know well the state of your flocks, and pay attention to your herds,

lessons.still: Think about the first money you spent this morning, even if it was just a cup of coffee or a bus fare. Say to the Lord: “Lord, even this small amount is something you entrusted to me. Teach me to be faithful in little things.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When the master returns he “settles accounts,” reminding us that the money is not ours and that one day we will give account to God. Applied to money, the “practice” and “review” steps of the eight steps for changing your mindset mean tracking our spending together, looking back together, and being faithful in a few things.
lessons.jesus: After five thousand people had eaten their fill, Jesus said to his disciples, “Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost” (John 6:12). The Lord who could turn five loaves and two fish into abundance still valued every leftover scrap. The God of abundance is also a God who wastes nothing.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, you value our faithfulness in a few things. Help us know clearly the state of our home, and stop using what you have entrusted to us carelessly. Let us track and review our spending together, not to blame each other, but so that one day we may hear you say, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” Amen.
teach: Jesus told a parable: before a master went on a journey he entrusted his money to his servants, and “after a long time the lord of those servants came, and settled accounts with them” (Matthew 25:19). The master praised the faithful servant: “You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matthew 25:21). What God values is not how much we manage, but how we manage it. Faithfulness does not begin with big donations or grand plans; it begins with small everyday expenses.

Proverbs says, “Know well the state of your flocks, and pay attention to your herds” (Proverbs 27:23). In ancient times, flocks and herds were a family’s wealth. In today’s terms: know clearly your household’s income, spending, debts and reserves. Many couples have only a vague sense of their finances until the end of the month, when they discover there isn’t enough. If things are unclear, it is hard to be faithful.

The simplest place to start is to track your spending together for one month. It doesn’t need to be complicated; just record every expense, and at the end of the month sit down together to look at it. The goal is not to catch the other person out, but to see together where the money is going. Just as a doctor takes your blood pressure before writing a prescription, household finances need to be seen clearly before a couple can make adjustments that please God.
q: On a scale of one to ten, how clearly do I know our monthly income and spending? Am I deliberately avoiding knowing?
With what kind of “small money” am I most careless, thinking it doesn’t matter?
talk: Are we willing to try tracking our spending together for a month? What method would be simplest for both of us?
When we look over the accounts at the end of the month, what attitude can we agree on so that we both feel safe?
acts: Starting today, record every expense, big or small
Agree with your spouse on a day at the end of the month to review the accounts together
Find one small expense you could cut
lessons.noon: “You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” — Lord, right now I want to be faithful to you in every small amount I spend today.

lessons.title: Providing for the Lord’s Household with Our Means
lessons.theme: When Jesus changes our lives, our wallets change too

v: Soon afterwards, he went about through cities and villages, preaching and bringing the good news of God’s Kingdom. With him were the twelve,
and certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out;
and Joanna, the wife of Chuzas, Herod’s steward; Susanna; and many others who served them from their possessions.

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus coming to your home tonight and sitting in your living room. How do you feel? Quietly say to the Lord: “Lord Jesus, welcome into our home, and into every corner of it, including our wallet.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: These women were not changed by attending a money-management class, but by meeting Jesus. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. When our view of money turns from “mine” to “God’s,” our home changes from a place where things pile up into a place where blessing flows out.
lessons.jesus: When the collectors of the temple tax came to Peter, Jesus told him to go fishing in the sea and find a coin in the mouth of the fish: “Take that, and give it to them for me and you” (Matthew 17:27). Jesus did not dodge his responsibilities, and he showed his disciples that the Father will provide for what we rightly owe.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for healing us and changing us first. Be King of our home, and Lord of our wallet too. Wherever we have responsibilities to meet, give us faithfulness to fulfill them; whatever you have entrusted to us, make us glad to use it to provide for your Kingdom and to bless others. Amen.
teach: Luke records that as Jesus traveled through towns and villages preaching, besides the twelve disciples there were some women with him. They had been troubled by evil spirits and illnesses, and Jesus had healed and transformed them. Luke says they were among “many others who served them from their possessions” (Luke 8:3). Behind the gospel ministry stood a group of people touched by grace, who gladly opened their wallets.

One of them was named Joanna, “the wife of Chuzas, Herod’s steward” (Luke 8:3). She was a married woman whose husband managed affairs in the royal household. We don’t know what her husband believed, but we see that, within her own family situation, she used her resources for God’s Kingdom. This reminds us: change your mindset and your life will change; change your life and your daily living will change, even where your money goes.

This week we have seen that money is God’s, that money reveals the heart, that couples need transparency, and that we must be faithful in small things. None of this is a set of financial rules; it is the natural result of meeting Jesus. When Jesus reigns in our home, money turns from “piling up for ourselves” to “providing for God’s Kingdom and blessing others.” Next week we will talk together about contentment, budgeting and debt.
q: If Jesus were living in our home today, what is the one thing about money I would most want to change?
How much of my resources is currently flowing toward God’s Kingdom and the needs of others?
talk: From this week’s lessons, what would you most like to change about our family’s view of money?
How could we together become a family that blessing flows out from? Think of one small, concrete way to start. If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down one step you could take yourself.
acts: Write down one action you want to take with money in response to Jesus
If you have any overdue bills, make a plan today to deal with them
Pray for someone in financial need, and think about how you could help
lessons.noon: “many others who served them from their possessions” — Lord Jesus, right now I want everything I have to be at your service.

26.title: Contentment and Managing Money as One

mem.t: But godliness with contentment is great gain.

s: If you haven’t yet, complete the “marriage check-up” together on the “Us” page in the app before heading out on your date.
Find a quiet place and take turns naming three changes in your spouse over the past six months that you are most grateful for, with specific events and times.
Look at your check-up results together and each pick one direction where you “want to grow together in the second half of the year.” Talk only about hopes; don’t dig up old grievances.
Read 1 Timothy 6:6 together, hold hands, and pray: “Lord, with you and with each other, we are content.”

lessons.title: Godliness with Contentment
lessons.theme: Contentment is not having more, but having enough in God

v: But godliness with contentment is great gain.
For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out.
But having food and clothing, we will be content with that.
But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction.
For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.

lessons.still: Grow quiet and count what you have right now: breath, clothes, a home to go back to, a person in your life. Say to the Lord: “Lord, thank you. Today, what I have is enough.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Discontent grows from the self-ruled life: I want more, I want to keep up with others, I want to be noticed. To be self-emptied is not to have nothing, but to enter into the limitless. Those who have God himself in Christ don’t need things to prove their worth.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “The foxes have holes and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay his head” (Luke 9:58). The Lord of all things had no house of his own on earth, yet he never lacked peace or joy. His satisfaction was not in possessions, but in the presence of his Father.
lessons.pray: Lord, giver of every good thing, you have already given us yourself, and each other. Forgive us for so often feeling it’s not enough and always wanting more. Teach us godliness with contentment, so that we find our satisfaction in you and keep thankfulness alive in our home. Amen.
teach: Paul says, “But godliness with contentment is great gain” (1 Timothy 6:6). The world says “more is great gain”; Scripture says “contentment is great gain.” Paul reminds us, “For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out” (1 Timothy 6:7). All the possessions of a lifetime are like the things we use during a hotel stay: at checkout, we can’t take any of them with us.

Wanting more is like drinking seawater: the more you drink, the thirstier you get. Ecclesiastes says, “He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver” (Ecclesiastes 5:10). Paul warns, “those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare” (1 Timothy 6:9). Many couples fight not because they lack, but because it “never feels like enough”: the house isn’t big enough, the income isn’t high enough, the kids don’t have enough tutoring. Discontent can wear a whole family out.
