Paul says, “But having food and clothing, we will be content with that” (1 Timothy 6:8). This doesn’t mean we shouldn’t work hard; it means we shouldn’t let our desires define our happiness. Contentment is the state of being satisfied by God: because we have God and each other, we are already rich. A contented home may not have the most, but it knows best how to give thanks, and how to enjoy what God has given.
q: In what area do I most often feel it’s “not enough”? Behind that feeling, what am I really looking for?
Have I made some material goal a condition for our family’s happiness?
talk: What do you think our family already has but often forgets to be thankful for?
For you, what does “our family already has enough” look like?
acts: Write down five things your family already has that are worth giving thanks for
Put off one “want, not need” purchase today
Tell your spouse: “With you, I feel rich.”
lessons.noon: “godliness with contentment is great gain” — Lord, right now I thank you that having you is enough.

lessons.title: The Secret of Not Comparing
lessons.theme: Contentment is learned, and the secret is strength from the Lord

v: Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.
I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In any and all circumstances I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.
I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.

lessons.still: Think about the photo or piece of news you saw today that stirred up comparison in your heart. Don’t push it down; bring it to the Lord and say: “Lord, I give my comparing heart to you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Comparison focuses on other people; complaining focuses on circumstances; neither focuses on Jesus. With our focus on Jesus, we see the grace he has already given. From a human point of view, other people always seem better off; from God’s point of view, what he has given our family is exactly what fits us best.
lessons.jesus: After Jesus restored Peter, Peter turned, saw John, and asked, “Lord, what about this man?” Jesus said, “what is that to you? You follow me” (John 21:22). Jesus brought Peter’s eyes back from someone else to focus on following his own calling.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, we confess that we often look at others and compare ourselves with them, and lose our thankfulness and joy. Bring our eyes back to you. Teach us the secret of contentment, to draw strength from you whether we have plenty or are in need. And help us never to compare our spouse with anyone else, but simply to treasure the one you have given. Amen.
teach: Comparing is easier today than ever. Open your phone and you see other people’s new cars, vacations, renovations and children’s awards. What we see are carefully chosen highlights, and we set them beside the ordinary days of our own lives; no wonder the more we compare, the less satisfied we are. Couples compare too: “Look how well her husband earns,” “Look how well his wife runs the house.” Comparison is contentment’s greatest enemy.

Paul says, “I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it” (Philippians 4:11). “Learned” tells us contentment is not inborn; it is practiced. Paul knew what it was “both to abound and to be in need” (Philippians 4:12). His secret was not in his circumstances but in this: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13). The context of this famous verse is, in fact, contentment.

How do we practice not comparing? First, look a little less: notice which content often makes you compare, and cut back on it sensibly. Second, count a little more: count God’s graces every day. Third, change the question: instead of asking “What do other people have?” ask “What has God given us?” Most important of all, never compare your spouse with anyone else. Every spouse is a tailor-made gift from God; they cannot be compared, only treasured.
q: Who do I most often compare our family with? How do I usually feel afterward?
Have I ever compared my spouse with someone else, in my heart or out loud?
talk: What kind of content or situation most easily starts you comparing? How can we remind each other?
Name one way you feel “our family is unique and blessed.”
acts: Today, skip one social-media feed that often makes you compare
Before bed, count three graces from today
Tell your spouse: “You are the one God made just for me.”
lessons.noon: “I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it” — Lord, right now I take my eyes off others and look only at the grace you have given.

lessons.title: First Sit Down and Count the Cost: Budgeting as One
lessons.theme: A budget is a couple telling their money, together, what God wants

v: For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?
Or perhaps, when he has laid a foundation and isn’t able to finish, everyone who sees begins to mock him,
saying, ‘This man began to build and wasn’t able to finish.’
The plans of the diligent surely lead to profit; and everyone who is hasty surely rushes to poverty.

lessons.still: Picture the two of you sitting side by side at the dining table with a blank sheet of paper in front of you. Don’t rush to the numbers; first say to the Lord: “Lord, before we write anything down, please come and sit between us.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When one person controls the finances alone, even with good intentions, it easily turns into “I’m in charge.” Budgeting is a way for a couple to practice letting Jesus reign together: being humble before the numbers, listening to each other and giving way to each other. Humility draws out humility, and both of you win.
lessons.jesus: Jesus taught his disciples, “Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself” (Matthew 6:34). He was not against planning; he himself said that someone building a tower should count the cost first. He wants us to trust our heavenly Father as we plan, doing our part without being bound by worry.
lessons.pray: Lord who gives wisdom, teach us to plan diligently, not hastily or carelessly. Help us sit down together with one heart and arrange the money you have entrusted to us according to your will. Before the numbers, let us be humble toward each other and listen to each other, so that budgeting becomes a practice of oneness and not the start of a fight. Amen.
teach: Jesus said, “For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?” (Luke 14:28). Jesus used building a tower to illustrate the cost of being his disciple, and it also shows us a principle for life: for important things, first sit down and count the cost. Building a home is like building a tower; without a budget, we often end up like the man who “began to build and wasn’t able to finish” (Luke 14:30).

Proverbs says, “The plans of the diligent surely lead to profit; and everyone who is hasty surely rushes to poverty” (Proverbs 21:5). A budget is not a shackle on our freedom. It makes our money follow our plans, instead of us chasing after our money. A simple household budget can start by listing monthly income and then dividing it among a few areas: giving, essential living costs, paying off debt, an emergency reserve, and the family’s leisure and growth.

The most important thing about a budget is not the numbers but being “of one mind.” You could hold a regular monthly family finance meeting: pray first, look at last month’s records, then decide together on next month’s plan. Each of you keeping a small amount of personal spending money that the other doesn’t ask about is also a way of respecting each other. No matter who is better with numbers or who earns more, the budget should be decided by both of you together.
q: When budgets come up, is my first reaction peace, pressure, or avoidance? Why?
In our household finances, do I want too much control, or have I gotten too used to pushing all the responsibility onto my spouse?
talk: If we made a household budget together, what item would you most want to keep or add?
What day of the month could we hold our family finance meeting? How can we keep it relaxed rather than tense?
acts: Set the time for your first family finance meeting with your spouse
Write down your monthly income and five main spending areas
Tell your spouse: “When it comes to money, we decide together.”
lessons.noon: “The plans of the diligent surely lead to profit” — Lord, right now please give us wisdom to arrange what you have entrusted to us with one heart.

lessons.title: Finding Freedom from Debt
lessons.theme: Facing our debt is the first step toward freedom

v: Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.
The rich rule over the poor. The borrower is servant to the lender.

lessons.still: If your family has debt, don’t be afraid right now, and don’t blame yourself. Picture it as a backpack, and gently set it down at the Lord’s feet. Say to him: “Lord, you know our situation. Please lead us.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Debt often begins with the self-ruled life: wanting more than we have now, wanting to look as good as everyone else. Seeing the temporary in the light of eternity, and turning from the world’s ways to God’s, we become willing to show restraint together for the sake of our family’s freedom. That is two people letting Jesus reign together.
lessons.jesus: Jesus once told a parable: “A certain lender had two debtors... he forgave them both” (Luke 7:41–42). The debt of sin we owe God is one we could never repay, yet Jesus paid it in full for us on the cross. People who have been forgiven a great debt can face their earthly debts with grace instead of shame.
lessons.pray: Gracious Lord, thank you for forgiving all our debt of sin on the cross. We place our family’s debts and pressures in your hands. Give us courage to face them together, wisdom to make a plan, and hearts of self-control. Don’t let us be bound by debt; let us find true freedom in you. Amen.
teach: Proverbs says, “The borrower is servant to the lender” (Proverbs 22:7). Debt takes away our freedom: each month’s paycheck belongs to someone else before it even arrives; we lie awake at night thinking about the bills. A great deal of stress and conflict between couples is tied to debt, and sometimes one spouse doesn’t even know how much the other owes. Debt is like an invisible rope that ties a family down.

Paul says, “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Romans 13:8). Paul wanted believers to pay what they owed on time and not keep others waiting. For a couple, there are three steps to begin: First, lay out all your debts together, listing how much you owe, the interest, and the monthly payments, without hiding anything and without blaming. Second, stop taking on new consumer debt, such as buying non-essential items in installments. Third, make a realistic repayment plan.

If your debt is already more than you can handle, don’t try to tough it out alone, and don’t believe the lure of “get rich quick” schemes. Seek advice from a trustworthy, mature believer at church, or turn to a legitimate, reliable debt-counseling or financial-advice service. Debt is a situation to be faced, not your identity. God can make a way in the hardest times, just as he once worked a miracle for the widow in debt.
q: How much do I really understand about our family’s debts? Am I avoiding certain numbers?
Is there any purchase or debt I took on because I wanted to look as good as everyone else?
talk: When it comes to debt, what is your biggest worry or source of stress? I want to listen first, not rush to fix it.
Can we set a time to list all our debts together? How will we promise each other not to blame?
acts: List all the debts you know of, ready to look at them with your spouse
This week, put one non-essential installment or credit-card purchase on hold
Pray for a friend or family member weighed down by debt
lessons.noon: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” — Lord, right now please set us free, so we find freedom in you.

lessons.title: Half-Year Review: A Marriage Check-Up
lessons.theme: We stop to take stock so we can move forward better

v: Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.
Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Today marks the midpoint of this year’s course. Grow quiet and think back over the twenty-six weeks you have walked through with your spouse. Say to the Lord: “Lord, thank you for walking with us all the way. Please search us, and lead us through the second half of the year.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Among the eight steps for changing your mindset, “review, adjust, repeat” cannot be skipped. When people with self on the throne look back, they see the other person’s shortcomings; self-emptied people ask first, “Lord, where do I need to change?” When change begins with me, our marriage will be renewed step by step.
lessons.jesus: When the seventy returned from their mission, they joyfully reported to Jesus. Jesus looked back with them, but reminded them to “rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). The review Jesus leads shifts our focus from achievement back to grace.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you for walking with us these six months and doing good work in our home. Shine your light on us, show us where we need to change, and heal our wounds. As we look back, we will not condemn each other, but turn to you together. Help us forget what is behind, stretch forward to what is ahead, and press on toward the goal. Amen.
teach: Today this year’s course reaches its halfway point. Over these six months we began with “God is the designer of marriage,” and saw that the self-ruled life is the root of conflict and that only the self-emptied life makes oneness possible. We learned what love really is and practiced the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. In recent weeks we have talked about the rhythms of home, and about money and stewardship. Week by week, fifteen minutes at a time, little by little, God has been at work in our home.

Just as people need regular health check-ups, marriages need check-ups too. The prophet says, “Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD” (Lamentations 3:40). Notice that it says “us,” and that it is “our” own ways being searched. A check-up is not for finding where our spouse falls short; it is for looking at our marriage together before God: where has there been growth, where is healing needed, and where must we keep practicing? This week, please complete a “marriage check-up” together on the “Us” page in the app.

Paul says, “one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal” (Philippians 3:13–14). We look back in order to move forward. When doing the check-up, pray for each other first; when looking at the results, give thanks for progress first, then gently talk about areas that need to grow. Past failures don’t need to be dragged up again and again, and seeing problems is no reason to lose heart, because God is still at work. There are twenty-six more weeks ahead, and the goal is Christ.
q: Over the past six months, what is the most obvious change in me in our marriage?
In what area is God still gently reminding me that I need to change?
talk: After completing the marriage check-up, name one way you have seen our family grow, and thank each other.

In the second half of the year, in what area would you most like us to grow together? Share one specific hope. If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down your hopes for them and for your marriage.
acts: Complete the marriage check-up with your spouse on the “Us” page in the app today
Write down the one thing you are most thankful for from these six months
Tell your spouse: “Thank you for walking with me these six months.”
lessons.noon: “forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before” — Lord, right now I let go of the past and move forward together with my spouse.

mem.t: Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

s: Think back together: who has generously blessed us this year? Each name one person and one thing they did, and thank God for them.
Lay out a sheet of paper and write “Our Family’s Giving” at the top. After praying together, decide what you will give this month to your church, to missions, or to help people in need.
Choose one person or family near you who is in need, and plan together an anonymous small gift or a meal for them.
Hold hands and read 2 Corinthians 9:7, then say to each other: “May our home be a home that gives cheerfully.”

lessons.title: First Giving Ourselves to the Lord
lessons.theme: Generosity starts not with our wallet but with giving ourselves to God

v: Moreover, brothers, we make known to you the grace of God which has been given in the assemblies of Macedonia,
how in a severe ordeal of affliction, the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded to the riches of their generosity.
For according to their power, I testify, yes and beyond their power, they gave of their own accord,
begging us with much entreaty to receive this grace and the fellowship in the service to the saints.
This was not as we had expected, but first they gave their own selves to the Lord, and to us through the will of God.
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.

lessons.still: Grow quiet and rest your open hands on your knees, as if holding up everything in them before the Lord. Say to him: “Lord, before we talk about money, I give myself to you once again.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: People with self on the throne ask, “If I give this, how much will I have left?” Self-emptied people first ask, “Whose am I?” Life first, then daily living: when we first give ourselves to the Lord and let Jesus reign, giving is no longer a painful loss but the natural overflow of love.
lessons.jesus: A boy had five barley loaves and two fish, and the disciples thought, “what are these among so many?” (John 6:9). But Jesus took them, and “having given thanks, he distributed” them to those who were sitting down (John 6:11). What Jesus values is not the amount but the heart that places it in his hands. Whatever we give him, he blesses, breaks, and uses to satisfy many.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, though you were rich, you became poor for us, so that through you we might become rich. Today we will not first count how much is in our hands; instead we give ourselves to you once again. Be Lord of our lives and Lord of our money, and by your grace make our home a home that gives cheerfully. Amen.
teach: Paul was writing to the wealthy church in Corinth, yet he held up the poor churches of Macedonia as an example. “In a severe ordeal of affliction, the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded to the riches of their generosity” (2 Corinthians 8:2). Amazingly, they even came “begging us with much entreaty” (2 Corinthians 8:4) for a share in serving the saints. Generosity is not reserved for the rich; it is the fruit that naturally flows from a heart touched by grace.

The key is in verse 5: “first they gave their own selves to the Lord” (2 Corinthians 8:5). Think of a fruit tree. If its roots are planted in good soil, bearing fruit comes naturally; if the roots are not planted well, fruit tied onto the branches is fake, no matter how much you tie on. The order of giving is the same: first the person, then the money. When our lives belong to the Lord, our wallets follow; if we are still running our own lives, giving easily becomes a burden or a transaction.

The source of this generosity is Jesus: “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). We do not give in order to earn grace; we give because we have already received grace. When a couple talks about giving, the best place to start is not with the numbers, but by coming back together to the cross and counting how much the Lord has already given our family.
q: If my life were a tree, are my roots planted in the Lord right now, or in “security,” “savings,” or “what other people think”?
The Lord “became poor” for our family. Which grace do I most want to thank him for?
talk: In the family you grew up in, what was giving like? Joyful, a rule, or something rarely talked about? How has that shaped the way you see giving today?
Think of a time when we experienced God’s provision even in our lack. What did we learn from it?
acts: Write down three graces our family has received because the Lord “became poor”
Pray a giving prayer together with your spouse: “Lord, first we give ourselves to you.”
Look for a chance today to bless someone without expecting anything back
lessons.noon: “first they gave their own selves to the Lord” — Lord, right now I give myself to you once again.

lessons.title: A Cheerful Giver
lessons.theme: God delights not in large, grudging sums but in a cheerful heart

v: Remember this: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work.

lessons.still: Picture a farmer standing at the edge of a field with seed in his hand. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, what seeds are in my hand that you want me to scatter?” Let your heart relax before the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Grudging giving means the “self” is still sitting on the throne, only forced by rules to give up a little; cheerful giving is the natural response of a heart that lets Jesus reign. Change your mindset and your life will change: the money is not something of “mine” being taken away, but something of “God’s” flowing out through our hands.
lessons.jesus: A woman broke an alabaster jar and poured very costly ointment on Jesus’ head, and the onlookers scolded her for the waste. But Jesus said, “Leave her alone... She has done a good work for me” (Mark 14:6). What Jesus saw was a loving heart that did not calculate but gave completely and gladly, and he said that she would be remembered wherever the good news is preached.
lessons.pray: Lord who supplies seed to the sower, thank you for making all grace abound to our family. Remove the reluctance, fear and calculating from our hearts, and give us cheerful hearts. Let us determine together, sow together, and see together how you cause thanksgiving to rise to your name. Amen.
teach: Paul uses an image every farmer understands: “he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully” (2 Corinthians 9:6). Throwing seed into the ground looks like “losing” it, but it is really “investing” it. A farmer who refuses to sow may seem to have kept his seed safe in the barn, but he will never see a harvest. Giving is like that: from a human point of view it is losing something; from God’s point of view it is sowing, and the harvest is the fruit of righteousness, along with many people’s thanks to God.

Then Paul says, “Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). “Determined” means thinking it through ahead of time and making a decision, not acting on a sudden impulse. The original word for “cheerful” carries the sense of glad and wholehearted. God does not need our money; what he wants is a joyful heart. If we give because we are pushed by guilt, pressure or saving face, however large the amount, God does not value it.

Verse 8 gives us a firm assurance: “God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work” (2 Corinthians 9:8). This is not a formula that says “give and you’ll get rich”; it is a promise that God will supply what we need so that we can “abound to every good work.” What God gives us is not only for storing up but for passing on. Our home is a pipe, not a reservoir.
q: When I give, what fills my heart more: joy and gratitude, or reluctance, guilt, and fear of what others will think?
If our home is a pipe rather than a reservoir, where is it clogged right now?
talk: Is our current giving something we “determined together in advance,” or is it more spontaneous, or decided by one of us? How would you like to adjust it?
If money weren’t a worry, which person or ministry would you most like us to bless together? Why?
acts: Set a time with your spouse to “determine” together this month’s giving
As you give, pray silently: “Lord, I gladly give this back to you.”
Write down the name of someone you would like to bless with money or time
lessons.noon: “God loves a cheerful giver” — Lord, right now please give me a cheerful heart.

lessons.title: The Widow’s Two Small Coins
lessons.theme: God looks not at how much we give, but at how much we keep

v: Jesus sat down opposite the treasury and saw how the multitude cast money into the treasury. Many who were rich cast in much.
A poor widow came and she cast in two small brass coins, which equal a quadrans coin.
He called his disciples to himself and said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, this poor widow gave more than all those who are giving into the treasury,
for they all gave out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, gave all that she had to live on.”

lessons.still: Picture the two of you sitting opposite the temple treasury, with Jesus sitting right beside you. Be still for a moment, and let his gentle gaze see your family’s real situation, and see your hearts.
lessons.light: 321 Light: From a human point of view, two small coins are hardly worth mentioning; from God’s point of view, they are complete trust. The focus is not on the amount, nor on how much others give, but on whether my heart puts God first. When God is God and I am his steward, even the smallest coin becomes worship.
lessons.jesus: Jesus did not only praise the widow for giving everything; he was that kind of giver himself. He said, “For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Not long after, on the cross, he gave everything he had.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, sitting opposite the treasury, thank you for valuing our smallest offerings and for seeing right through our hearts. Forgive us for so often giving you what is left over and keeping the best for ourselves. Teach us to honor you first by faith, and whether we have plenty or are in need, to be faithful stewards before you. Amen.
teach: Jesus “sat down opposite the treasury and saw how the multitude cast money into the treasury” (Mark 12:41). Notice that Jesus was watching not only how much people gave, but “how” they gave. The rich put in large sums, with plenty of noise; a poor widow quietly put in two small coins, something almost anyone would overlook. But Jesus deliberately called his disciples over, pointed to this unremarkable woman, and said she “gave more than all those who are giving into the treasury” (Mark 12:43).

Why? Jesus explained: “they all gave out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, gave all that she had to live on” (Mark 12:44). Heaven counts differently from earth: earth looks at the amount; heaven looks at the proportion and the faith. This is a huge comfort to families who are financially stretched: your small offerings are not small at all in God’s eyes. And it is a gentle reminder to families who are comfortable: giving “out of our abundance” may still weigh very little in God’s eyes.

Scripture also teaches us to “Honor the LORD with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase” (Proverbs 3:9). “First fruits” means giving to God first, not giving him whatever is left over at the end. It is like serving the first bowl of rice at the table to the eldest, as a sign of honor. Many Christian families use a tenth as a starting point to learn to “give to God first”; what matters even more is the order: before paying the bills, before buying what we want, we first give honor to God.
q: Am I in the habit of giving God the “first fruits,” or only giving him “what’s left”? How can I tell?
Have I ever felt ashamed because I gave little, or secretly proud because I gave a lot? How does the Lord see these two attitudes?
talk: If our family practiced “giving to God first,” which would be hardest to give first: money, time, or energy? Why?
Is our family’s financial situation right now more like “abundance” or “poverty”? In this situation, what kind of giving would be sincere and full of faith for us?
acts: When the first income of this month comes in, set aside your giving before dealing with anything else
Tell your spouse one way you appreciate their generosity
Today, give someone something that is your “best” rather than your “leftovers”
lessons.noon: “Honor the LORD with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase” — Lord, right now I want to give you my best first.

lessons.title: Both Men and Women, Willing-Hearted
lessons.theme: When a couple decides on giving together, they find joy in being of one heart

v: They came, everyone whose heart stirred him up, and everyone whom his spirit made willing, and brought the LORD’s offering for the work of the Tent of Meeting, and for all of its service, and for the holy garments.

They came, both men and women, as many as were willing-hearted, and brought brooches, earrings, signet rings, and armlets, all jewels of gold; even every man who offered an offering of gold to the LORD.
They spoke to Moses, saying, “The people have brought much more than enough for the service of the work which the LORD commanded to make.”

Moses gave a commandment, and they caused it to be proclaimed throughout the camp, saying, “Let neither man nor woman make anything else for the offering for the sanctuary.” So the people were restrained from bringing.
For the stuff they had was sufficient to do all the work, and too much.

lessons.still: Picture the two of you walking hand in hand toward God’s tent, carrying the gifts you will offer. Quietly say to the Lord: “Lord, together we want to give you what is in our hands.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: If one spouse “rules the roost” over giving, it easily becomes a tug-of-war; when husband and wife decide together before God and let Jesus reign, giving becomes a practice of oneness. Humility draws out humility: first listen to your spouse’s thoughts, then obey God’s prompting together, and your home will be blessed in being of one heart.
lessons.jesus: After meeting Jesus, Zacchaeus “stood and said to the Lord, ‘Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much’” (Luke 19:8). No one forced him; he was changed by Jesus’ acceptance. Jesus shows us that true generosity is willing-hearted, and that it always goes hand in hand with honesty and joy.
lessons.pray: Lord who moves people’s hearts, thank you for placing a willing-hearted prompting within us. Keep us from each doing our own thing when it comes to giving; let us pray together, determine together, and offer together. May our family’s gifts, added to the offerings of everyone in your household, become a dwelling place for your presence, and may we find joy in being of one heart. Amen.
teach: When the Israelites built the Tent of Meeting in the wilderness, Moses did not assign quotas or apply pressure. Scripture says: “They came, everyone whose heart stirred him up, and everyone whom his spirit made willing, and brought the LORD’s offering” (Exodus 35:21). Then comes a moving detail: “They came, both men and women, as many as were willing-hearted” (Exodus 35:22), bringing brooches, earrings, signet rings and armlets. These were mostly personal jewelry, quite possibly a family’s most treasured keepsakes, yet men and women, household by household, offered them with one heart.

Giving as a couple is the same; at its most beautiful it is “both men and women”: not one spouse giving on impulse while the other worries in the background, nor one quietly holding back while the other is kept in the dark. You can pray together, look at your household income and spending together, and then decide together how much to give this month and this year, and where. If your views differ, start from where you are both “willing-hearted,” without forcing or comparing, and grow slowly in unity.

And the result? The people brought “much more than enough,” so that Moses even had to send out a command: “Let neither man nor woman make anything else for the offering for the sanctuary” (Exodus 36:6). It is a rare picture in Scripture: so much was given that it had to be stopped! When God moves people’s hearts and household after household gives willingly, God’s work will never lack. Our family’s giving may seem small, but added to the offerings of everyone in God’s household, it becomes a dwelling place for God’s presence.
q: When it comes to our family’s giving, do I tend to decide on my own and inform my spouse, or am I willing to pray and decide together?
If I were asked to offer something “personal and precious,” what would I find hardest to let go of? What does that reveal?
talk: Have we ever disagreed about giving without saying so? Please share gently, using “I wish…” rather than “You always…”.

If we were to build a habit of “deciding our giving together,” how often would you like to talk about it, and in what way? (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down what you would like to discuss with them.)
acts: Set a time with your spouse for your next “deciding our giving together” conversation
First ask your spouse: “What is God stirring in your heart about giving?”
When you give, don’t make a show of it; just say in your heart: “Lord, this is from us to you.”
lessons.noon: “everyone whose heart stirred him up, and everyone whom his spirit made willing” — Lord, right now please move us to give with one heart and a willing spirit.

lessons.title: A Generous Home
lessons.theme: Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also: let our home be an outlet of blessing

v: “Don’t be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the Kingdom.
Sell what you have and give gifts to the needy. Make for yourselves purses which don’t grow old, a treasure in the heavens that doesn’t fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys.
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
But don’t forget to be doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.

lessons.still: Look around your home: the dining table, the couch, the front door. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, let this home be not only our shelter from the storm, but also a place where others experience your grace.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. A generous home treats things as tools for building relationships, rather than treating people as threats to its things. When we turn from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, our home is building God’s order and storing up treasure that never fails.
lessons.jesus: Jesus taught a host: “when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind; and you will be blessed” (Luke 14:13–14). He himself often ate with people who were shut out. Jesus’ generosity opened the table to people who could never repay, because his reward is in heaven.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that it is your good pleasure to give the Kingdom to us, your little flock. Remove the fear from our hearts, and let our hearts rest in your Kingdom. Let our home often open its door and stretch out its hands, blessing others with our money, our time and our table, so that people see your generosity and goodness in our home. Amen.
teach: Jesus said, “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Luke 12:34). We often assume that wherever our heart is, our money will follow; but Jesus says the reverse is also true: wherever we put our money, our heart will be drawn there. It is like someone who buys shares in a company and starts following its news every day. When our family invests money in God’s Kingdom, our hearts will care more and more about the people God cares about.

Before saying this, Jesus said, “Don’t be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the Kingdom” (Luke 12:32). The biggest obstacle to generosity is often not greed but fear: fear of not having enough, fear of the future, fear for our children’s needs. Jesus first comforts our fear, then calls us to generosity. If our heavenly Father is pleased to give us the Kingdom itself, would he forget our daily needs?

Generosity is not only about giving money. Hebrews reminds us: “But don’t forget to be doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased” (Hebrews 13:16). A hot meal, a guest room, time spent keeping someone company, a ride somewhere: all of these can be sacrifices offered to God. This week we began with “first giving ourselves to the Lord,” then learned to give cheerfully, to give to God first, and to decide on giving as one. Finally, let all of this become our family’s culture: a home whose door is often open and whose hands are often outstretched.
q: Looking at our family’s recent spending, where is our “treasure” mostly going? What does that reveal about where my heart is?
What holds me back from generosity more: greed or fear? What am I most afraid of?
talk: Which lesson about giving this week touched you most? What one concrete change would you like to see in our family’s generosity?
If our home is to become an “outlet of blessing,” what small step would you most like to start with: at our table, with our time, or with our money?
acts: Choose together one person or family to bless this week
Invite someone who is rarely invited out for a simple home-cooked meal
Write down one need you most worry “won’t be enough,” and entrust it to your heavenly Father
lessons.noon: “where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” — Lord, right now I place my heart and my treasure in your Kingdom.

mem.t: The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.

s: Set aside a stretch of uninterrupted time: switch off your phones, dim the lights, brew a pot of tea or make a warm drink. This time belongs to just the two of you.
Take turns finishing this sentence: “The moment I feel most safe and accepted with you is when…”
Hold hands or lean against each other and quietly listen to a worship song you both love. No need to rush into talking; simply enjoy being together.
Read Genesis 2:25 together. Thank God for the gift of intimacy, and ask him to keep drawing you closer in body, heart, and spirit.

lessons.title: Naked and Not Ashamed
lessons.theme: To be fully seen and still fully accepted was God’s design from the beginning

v: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.
The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.

lessons.still: Take a deep breath and let your body relax. Picture yourself back in Eden, a place with no masks and no hiding. Whisper to the Lord, “Lord, thank you for seeing all of me and loving me still.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shame and hiding only appeared after sin entered the world. When self is on the throne, we are afraid to be seen, so we cover up, defend, and control. Self-emptied people, accepted in Christ, are free to take off their masks. A home where Jesus reigns is a home where both can feel safe being “seen.”
lessons.jesus: Jesus told his disciples, “I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you” (John 15:15). Jesus did not just give his disciples orders; he opened his heart to them. His example shows us that intimacy begins with being willing to open up and be known.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, our Creator, thank you for bringing us to each other with your own hands and for designing the beautiful gift of intimacy. Heal the shame and fear in our hearts, so that we can take off our masks before each other, being seen and being accepted. May our home return to your original goodness in body, heart, and spirit. Amen.
teach: Genesis 2 ends with one short sentence about the first married couple: “The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25). This is not only about bodies; it describes the state of a relationship: fully seen, yet unafraid; nothing covered, and no fear of being mocked, compared, or used. Like a child who can simply be himself in front of parents who love him. This is the security God prepared for husband and wife.

Where does that security come from? From God’s way of seeing. After God made man and woman, “God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). The human body, our being male and female, the bond between two people: God called all of it “very good.” The body is not shameful, and intimacy is not dirty. When a husband and wife look at each other through God’s eyes, with appreciation rather than fault-finding, each one dares to lower their defenses, and intimacy finds room to grow.

This week we are talking about intimacy. Scripture describes the “one flesh” of marriage in three dimensions: closeness of body, knowing of heart, and walking together in spirit. The three are like a cord of three strands, woven into one another. In many cultures, sex is a taboo topic no one talks about; but the Bible tells us that intimacy is God’s blessing, not something to be ashamed of. We can talk about it with modesty, respect, and gratitude, because it is a good thing God himself designed.
q: Is there any part of me that, in front of my spouse, is still used to “wearing armor” and doesn’t dare let him or her see?
How much of my view of intimacy or sex has been shaped by a family or culture that treated it as shameful and not to be talked about?
talk: Think back to when we first met or were newly married. What did you appreciate most about me then? And what new good things do you see in me now?
In our relationship, what kind of moments make you feel most free to be yourself, with nothing to hide?
acts: Today, appreciate your spouse in one sentence: “I’m so grateful God brought you to me, because…”
Write down one small thing about yourself you’d like your spouse to know better
Give your spouse a gentle hug that comes with no expectations at all
lessons.noon: “God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good” — Lord, right now give me your eyes to appreciate my spouse.

lessons.title: The Safety of Being Known
lessons.theme: Emotional intimacy means knowing each other and accepting each other

v: LORD, you have searched me, and you know me.
You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar.
You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways.
For there is not a word on my tongue, but behold, LORD, you know it altogether.

lessons.still: Read this quietly once: “LORD, you have searched me, and you know me.” Let the words slowly sink to the bottom of your heart. God knows everything in your deepest places, and he has not left you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: With self on the throne, we want others to understand us first, but have little interest in understanding them. The self-emptied are willing to be the first to know and the first to accept. When the focus shifts from “Why don’t you understand me?” to “How can I get to know you better?”, intimacy begins to grow at home.
lessons.jesus: After meeting Jesus, the Samaritan woman ran back to town and said, “Come, see a man who told me everything that I have done” (John 4:29). Jesus knew her whole past, yet he did not humiliate her; instead he revealed himself to her. Being known by Jesus brings not shame, but new life and joy.
lessons.pray: All-knowing and loving Lord, thank you for knowing us completely and loving us still. Make our home a safe place, where we are willing to be known and willing to know each other with curiosity and tenderness. Wherever there is distance between our hearts, draw us close yourself, so that we may be truly one in heart. Amen.
teach: David said, “LORD, you have searched me, and you know me” (Psalm 139:1). God knows when we sit down and rise up, where we walk and when we lie down; even “there is not a word on my tongue, but behold, LORD, you know it altogether” (Psalm 139:4). To be known that completely could be terrifying; yet David bursts into praise, because the One who knows him also loves him deeply. Only people who are loved dare to be known.

Emotional intimacy is this experience of “being known and still accepted” between husband and wife. Many couples live together for years, familiar with each other’s routines, tastes, and habits, yet never learn the real fears, dreams, and wounds in each other’s hearts. It is like two people living on different floors of the same house, passing each other every day but rarely truly meeting. Bodies can be very close while hearts are far apart.

How do we build emotional intimacy? Start with curiosity, asking the way we did when we were dating: “What’s weighing on your heart most today?” Then add acceptance: when your spouse shares a weakness, don’t rush to correct it, and never use it as a weapon in an argument. Every safe response is a “trust deposit” in your marriage. As God gently knows us, we learn to know each other in the same way.
q: Am I like someone living on a different floor, familiar with my spouse’s habits but not really knowing his or her heart?
When my spouse tells me about a weakness, is my usual response acceptance, or correction and lecturing?
talk: Is there something that has been on your mind lately that you haven’t had a chance to tell me? I’ll listen quietly and not rush to give advice.
In what area would you like me to know you better? For example, your dreams, your fears, or something that happened when you were little.
acts: Today, ask your spouse a question you have never asked before
When your spouse shares, say “Thank you for telling me” first, before anything else
Write down three things you have recently learned about your spouse
lessons.noon: “LORD, you have searched me, and you know me” — Lord, right now thank you for knowing me and loving me still.

lessons.title: Physical Intimacy Is God’s Blessing
lessons.theme: Marital intimacy is a gift of faithfulness, delight, and mutual cherishing

v: Drink water out of your own cistern, running water out of your own well.
Should your springs overflow in the streets, streams of water in the public squares?
Let them be for yourself alone, not for strangers with you.
Let your spring be blessed. Rejoice in the wife of your youth.

lessons.still: Be still, and thank God for the body he has given you. Whether your body is healthy or frail, young or old, tell the Lord, “Lord, thank you. My body, too, is something you created and value.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Intimacy with self on the throne says, “I want to be satisfied.” Self-emptied intimacy says, “I want to bring you joy.” When the focus turns from my own needs to my spouse’s feelings, intimacy moves from taking to giving, from draining to nourishing, and becomes a beautiful expression of the mystery of being one.
lessons.jesus: Faced with a man with leprosy whom everyone avoided, Jesus responded: “Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him” (Mark 1:41). Jesus could have healed him with a single word, yet he chose to touch him. He shows us that a gentle touch carries acceptance and respect, and that physical closeness can convey deep love.
lessons.pray: Lord, Creator of our bodies, thank you for giving intimacy to husband and wife as a gift. Cleanse the way we think about intimacy; take away shame, selfishness, and fear, so that we delight in each other faithfully and honor each other tenderly. Heal the hurts of the past yourself, and guard this well of ours, so that it belongs only to us and is blessed by you. Amen.
teach: Proverbs uses a picture that people in desert lands understand best: “Drink water out of your own cistern, running water out of your own well” (Proverbs 5:15). Where water is scarce, a well that belongs to your own household is a huge blessing, something to protect, treasure, and not share with outsiders. A wise father uses this image to teach his son that the intimacy of marriage is a precious well: “Let them be for yourself alone, not for strangers with you” (Proverbs 5:17).

He goes on: “Let your spring be blessed. Rejoice in the wife of your youth” (Proverbs 5:18). The Bible doesn’t only say “don’t”; it also says “rejoice.” Physical intimacy is not only for having children, nor is it a reluctant duty. It is God’s gift to husband and wife to express love, build oneness, and comfort each other. God is a God of joy; he designed delight into marriage and blesses husband and wife as they enjoy each other in it.

The intimacy God designed has several marks. It is exclusive, kept within the covenant of marriage. It is mutual: both are respected and both are willing. It is gentle, caring about the other’s feelings more than one’s own needs. Any coercion, humiliation, or exploitation is never God’s will. If past experiences have filled this area with pain or difficulty, you don’t have to carry it alone; seek help from a mature pastor or a professional counselor. God is willing to heal and willing to make new.
q: Do I hold any unbiblical views about physical intimacy, such as thinking it dirty or shameful, or something only one of us needs?
When it comes to intimacy, do I think more often about my own needs or about my spouse’s feelings?
talk: Apart from sexual intimacy, what kind of physical touch makes you feel most loved? For example, holding hands, a hug, leaning on a shoulder, or a goodnight kiss.
In this area, how would you like us to care for each other’s feelings more gently? (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down what you would like to say to him or her.)
acts: Today, take your spouse’s hand first, or give a gentle hug
Pray once for your spouse’s physical health and peace of heart
Tell your spouse: “I really treasure the intimacy between us.”
lessons.noon: “Rejoice in the wife of your youth” — Lord, right now keep our love fresh and blessed.

lessons.title: Spiritual Intimacy: Fearing God Together
lessons.theme: The deepest oneness is two people standing together before God

v: There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judea, a certain priest named Zacharias, of the priestly division of Abijah. He had a wife of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.
They were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.
Then those who feared the LORD spoke one with another; and the LORD listened and heard, and a book of memory was written before him for those who feared the LORD and who honored his name.

lessons.still: If you can, sit side by side with your spouse; if you are alone, hold your spouse’s name in your heart. Say quietly, “Lord, we come before you together.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Without God at the center, physical and emotional intimacy easily turn into demands on each other. When husband and wife fear God together, the focus moves from “How much are you giving me?” to “To whom do we both belong?” Only when we let Jesus reign is the cord of three strands truly woven together.
lessons.jesus: Jesus “took with him Peter, John, and James, and went up onto the mountain to pray” (Luke 9:28), and there they saw the Lord’s glory. Jesus did not only pray by himself; he invited those close to him to pray with him. He shows us that the deepest togetherness is coming before the Father together and seeing God’s glory together.
lessons.pray: Lord who listens and hears, thank you for being the center of our marriage. Take away the spiritual awkwardness and distance between us, so that we can come before you side by side, talk with each other about your grace, and see each other’s longing and tears. Like Zacharias and Elizabeth, may the two of us fear you together before you. Amen.
teach: Luke’s Gospel opens by introducing a couple, Zacharias and Elizabeth: “They were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord” (Luke 1:6). Notice that the Bible says “both”: not one spiritual partner and one tagging along. Through long years of waiting and disappointment, they kept fearing God together. Their marriage had a shared center: God himself.

Spiritual intimacy is the deepest layer of a marriage, and also the most often neglected. Some couples eat together, manage money together, and sleep in the same bed, yet have never prayed or read the Bible together. It is like two candles burning separately: both give light, but they never become one flame. When two people come before God together and each sees the other’s most genuine worship, tears, and longing, that closeness cannot be replaced by anything else.

The prophet Malachi paints a beautiful picture: “Then those who feared the LORD spoke one with another; and the LORD listened and heard” (Malachi 3:16). When those who fear God talk with each other about him, God not only listens; he has their names written in a book of memory. Spiritual intimacy doesn’t require long speeches. It can begin with a very small step: giving thanks together before a meal, holding hands to say one sentence of prayer before bed, sharing a verse you read today. If your spouse can’t walk this path with you yet, you can begin by keeping watch for him or her before God; God values your faithfulness and will watch over your home.
q: In our marriage, which of the three kinds of intimacy (physical, emotional, spiritual) is strongest? Which is weakest?
What keeps my spouse and me from praying together? Busyness, awkwardness, fear of showing weakness, or something else?
talk: If we were to start (or deepen) a habit of praying together, what time and what way would feel most natural for us?
Is there something recently that you would like me to pray about for you?
acts: Tonight before bed, hold hands and each say a short prayer
Ask your spouse: “What can I pray for you about today?”
Share the verse that has touched you most this week
lessons.noon: “those who feared the LORD spoke one with another; and the LORD listened and heard” — Lord, right now hear us as we talk with each other about your word.

lessons.title: Bold and Unafraid, No Longer Ashamed
lessons.theme: God removes fear and shame so that couples can talk about intimacy with peace

v: I sought the LORD, and he answered me, and delivered me from all my fears.
They looked to him, and were radiant. Their faces shall never be covered with shame.
For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.
Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.

lessons.still: Put your hand on your heart and consider: in an intimate relationship, what am I most afraid of? Being rejected, laughed at, compared, or losing myself? Gently hand that fear over to the God who is love.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Fear often comes from the self: fear of losing face, fear of being hurt. Through the gospel, Jesus has already borne our punishment, and we no longer live in the fear of condemnation. The self-emptied, secure in the Lord, can be the first to offer safety and the first to open their hearts.
lessons.jesus: The disciples had locked the doors out of fear. Then “Jesus came and stood in the middle and said to them, ‘Peace be to you.’” (John 20:19), and he showed them the wounds in his hands and side. He did not rebuke their weakness; with a love that bore scars, he took away their fear and brought them joy.
lessons.pray: Lord, you who sympathize with our weaknesses, thank you that we can come before you boldly and without fear. Deliver us from all our fears and shame, and make our home a safe place where we can speak honestly and gently about each other’s needs. Guard our intimacy in body, heart, and spirit, so that we look to you and are no longer ashamed before each other. Amen.
teach: The greatest enemy of intimacy is often not a lack of love but fear: fear that voicing a need will be met with rejection, fear that sharing feelings will be misunderstood, fear of not being good enough. Fear makes us shut the door and build walls. David testified, “I sought the LORD, and he answered me, and delivered me from all my fears” (Psalm 34:4). And again, “They looked to him, and were radiant. Their faces shall never be covered with shame” (Psalm 34:5). Fear and shame are exactly the intimacy-killers we have kept meeting this week, and God can deliver us from both.

Where does this security come from? Hebrews tells us that we don’t have a high priest “who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities” (Hebrews 4:15), and so we are invited: “Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16). Before God we don’t have to pretend; we can come with our weakness and receive mercy and grace. When we are sure we are fully accepted by God, we no longer need our spouse’s reactions to decide our worth. Rejection won’t crush us, and when misunderstood we won’t rush to strike back.

So how can a couple talk about intimacy in a modest and fitting way? Choose a time when you are relaxed, not tired, and not just after an argument. Use “I feel… I hope…” instead of “You never…”. Express more appreciation than complaint. When you hear a different opinion, first say, “Thank you for being willing to tell me.” If some topics are too hard to say out loud, write them down first and hand them to your spouse. Just as God lets us come boldly and without fear before him, let us make it possible for our spouse to come to us boldly and without fear.
q: In our intimate relationship, what fear do I feel most often? How does it make me react?
Have I ever made my spouse feel, “If I say it, I’ll be blamed”? How can I give him or her more sense of safety?
talk: This week we have talked about physical, emotional, and spiritual intimacy. In which of these would you most like us to take one more step together?
Is there something about our intimacy that you have long wanted to say but haven’t dared to? If you can’t say it now, let’s agree on a time for you to write it to me.
acts: Tell your spouse: “Whatever you say, I want to listen well first.”
Use “I feel… I hope…” to express one small need
Write a one-sentence prayer thanking God for taking away your fear
lessons.noon: “They looked to him, and were radiant. Their faces shall never be covered with shame” — Lord, right now I look to you; take away my shame and fear.

mem.t: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the bed be undefiled; but God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.

date.t: Mending the Fence Around Our Garden
s: Go for a walk or share a drink together, and take turns saying: “In our marriage, what I most want to treasure and protect is…”
Sit down and, in a relaxed and non-blaming way, agree on three “fences for our home” together, for example around phones, friendships with the opposite sex, and evening routines.
Exchange a promise: “If I am weak or tempted, I will tell you first, and I will seek help.”
With your hand on your spouse’s hand, read Hebrews 13:4 and pray together: “Lord, be the watchman over our marriage.”

lessons.title: Let Marriage Be Held in Honor
lessons.theme: To honor marriage is to wholeheartedly guard the garden God has given us

v: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the bed be undefiled; but God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.
Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.”

lessons.still: Imagine your marriage as a garden, with flowers, fruit trees, and a fence around it. Quietly ask the Lord, “Lord, is our fence still whole today? Where does it need mending?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When we treat marriage as “mine,” we easily look elsewhere when we feel unsatisfied. When we treat it as something God has entrusted to us, we guard it carefully, like a steward. Let God be God: the dignity of marriage comes from the God who established it, not from how I feel at this moment.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus saw the temple turned into a marketplace, he drove out those who were buying and selling, and his disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will eat me up” (John 2:17). Jesus burned with protective zeal for the holy place God had established. He shows us that when we love what God loves, we will guard it with all our hearts.
lessons.pray: Lord, who established marriage, thank you for giving us this covenant and making it a precious treasure. Forgive us for the times we have made light of marriage, and forgive our discontented hearts. Be the watchman over our garden; help us mend the fence together, treasure each other in you, and stay faithful for life. Amen.
teach: Hebrews says, “Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the bed be undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4). The word for “honor” carries the sense of “precious, of great value,” the way we would treat a family heirloom. And notice: “among all.” Not only the husband and wife themselves, but everyone around them. Marriage is not merely a private matter between two people; it is a covenant established by God that the whole community should value.

Last week we saw that intimacy is God’s beautiful gift; precisely because it is precious, it needs guarding. A garden without a fence is open to wild animals, thieves, wind, and sand, and even the loveliest flowers won’t last long. A fence does not restrict freedom; it protects what is good. Many marriages are not breached overnight. The fence loosens bit by bit, until one day we discover the garden has gone to ruin.

Interestingly, the very next verse says, “Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have” (Hebrews 13:5). Whether it is money or desire, the root problem is discontent: feeling that what I have is not enough and always wanting what belongs to someone else. The first fence that guards a marriage is a contented, grateful heart: treasuring the one God has already given me, and trusting his promise: “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).
q: Do I treat marriage as a precious covenant to be “held in honor among all”? In my words, entertainment, and jokes, is there anywhere I make light of marriage?
Is there a corner of discontent in my heart that leads me to keep comparing my spouse with others?
talk: If our marriage were a garden, which part of the fence do you think is sturdiest right now? Which part do we need to mend together? Please speak in terms of “we,” without blaming each other.
Which people or settings around us help us honor our marriage? Which might be wearing it down?
acts: Today, tell your spouse: “I really treasure our marriage.”
Notice whether the entertainment or jokes you encounter today make light of marriage
Write down three things you are thankful for about “the one God has given me”
lessons.noon: “Let marriage be held in honor among all” — Lord, right now help me treasure the marriage you have given me.

lessons.title: Guard Your Heart
lessons.theme: Guarding a marriage starts with guarding the heart, turning back while things are still small

v: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.
Put away from yourself a perverse mouth. Put corrupt lips far from you.
Let your eyes look straight ahead. Fix your gaze directly before you.
Make the path of your feet level. Let all of your ways be established.
Don’t turn to the right hand nor to the left. Remove your foot from evil.

lessons.still: Be still, and picture your heart as a door. Ask the Lord, “Lord, what has quietly slipped in through this door lately?” Don’t rush to answer; let the Holy Spirit gently shine his light on you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself. Relying on willpower alone (“Don’t think about it!”) often makes the pull stronger the harder we push it down. When we let the Holy Spirit govern our hearts and let Jesus reign there, old cravings are replaced by a better love. The wellspring of life flows from the heart, and so does the fruit of a marriage.
lessons.jesus: Jesus taught that “everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). Jesus looks not only at behavior but at the heart. This is not meant to crush us under guilt, but to help us see that true guarding starts in the heart, and he came precisely to give us a new heart.
lessons.pray: Lord, who searches our hearts, create in us a clean heart and stand guard at the door of our hearts. Shine your light on every thought and desire that has quietly slipped in and does not belong to you, and remove it. When we are lonely or disappointed, help us come to you first and bravely open up to each other, so that our hearts belong wholly to you and to each other. Amen.
teach: Solomon said, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). To “keep” here means to watch over, to stand guard, like a sentry at the city gate. An affair or an addiction seldom begins with behavior; it begins in the heart: a thought, a fantasy, a comparison, a flicker of dissatisfaction that, left unchecked, slowly grows.

He goes on to speak of the mouth, the eyes, and the feet: “Let your eyes look straight ahead” (Proverbs 4:25); “Make the path of your feet level” (Proverbs 4:26). This is very practical wisdom: what our eyes look at and where our feet go both shape the heart. It is like driving: if the steering wheel is off by just a little and you never correct it, over a long drive you end up far off course. Guarding the heart means turning back while you are only a little off.

Guarding the heart does not mean suppressing feelings. Marriage has seasons of loneliness, disappointment, and feeling unappreciated; those feelings are real and need to be faced. The danger is taking them to the wrong place for comfort. A better direction is to pour them out before God and to bravely tell your spouse. A need that is spoken is far less likely to become a breach for temptation than a need that is hidden.
q: Lately, are there thoughts, comparisons, or fantasies in my heart that are “just a little off course” and need turning back right now?
When I feel lonely or disappointed in my marriage, where do I usually take those feelings?
talk: Have there been times recently when you felt lonely, unappreciated, or overlooked in our relationship? I want to listen well, without defending myself.
How can we make it easier for each other to voice the needs in our hearts, instead of hiding them?
acts: Write down one thought or habit that pulls your heart off course, and hand it over to the Lord
Today, tell your spouse about one small need instead of keeping it bottled up
Pray before bed: “Lord, guard my heart today.”
lessons.noon: “Keep your heart with all diligence” — Lord, right now stand guard at the door of my heart.

lessons.title: Boundaries with the Opposite Sex
lessons.theme: Clear boundaries are not distrust; they protect each other

v: After these things, his master’s wife set her eyes on Joseph; and she said, “Lie with me.”
But he refused, and said to his master’s wife, “Behold, my master doesn’t know what is with me in the house, and he has put all that he has into my hand.
No one is greater in this house than I am, and he has not kept back anything from me but you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
As she spoke to Joseph day by day, he didn’t listen to her, to lie by her, or to be with her.
About this time, he went into the house to do his work, and there were none of the men of the house inside.
She caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me!” He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.
the elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, in all purity.

lessons.still: Think about the people of the opposite sex you interact with in a day: coworkers, classmates, brothers and sisters at church, friends online. Bless them, and quietly ask the Lord, “Lord, give me wisdom to keep every relationship pure.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: With self on the throne we think, “I know my limits; I don’t need boundaries.” That is really pride, overestimating ourselves. Humble people admit they can be weak, so they put safeguards in place ahead of time. “Pride goes before destruction” (Proverbs 16:18); when we humbly return to our rightful place, we find true freedom instead.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he didn’t debate the devil; he refused firmly with God’s word: “Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.’” (Matthew 4:10). Jesus’ example tells us that we don’t need to negotiate with temptation; we stand clearly and decisively on God’s word.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you for the example of Joseph, which shows us how those who fear you face temptation. Give us humility to admit our weakness, wisdom to keep our relationships with the opposite sex pure, and trust in each other as we set boundaries together and keep them together. Keep our hearts wholly yours and wholly each other’s. Amen.
teach: In Egypt, Joseph was enticed by his master’s wife day after day, and his answer was clear: “How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” (Genesis 39:9). He saw not only the wrong he would do to his master, but the sin against God. The passage goes on to say that “he didn’t listen to her, to lie by her, or to be with her” (Genesis 39:10). Joseph didn’t only refuse the act; he avoided the situations that would make temptation stronger. When she finally grabbed his garment, he would rather leave it behind and “ran outside.”

Boundaries with the opposite sex don’t mean treating every man or woman as a danger; they mean relating in fitting ways. Paul tells Timothy to treat “the younger as sisters, in all purity” (1 Timothy 5:2). In practice that can mean: not spending long stretches alone in private with the same person of the opposite sex; not confiding your marriage frustrations to someone of the opposite sex; keeping your private messages and calls such that you wouldn’t mind your spouse seeing them; and being on alert when you find yourself looking forward to seeing someone or caring a lot about their replies. An emotional affair usually begins well before a physical one.

Boundaries are best set by husband and wife together, not demanded or policed by one side. Excessive suspicion and control can themselves harm a marriage. Healthy boundaries are like a shared promise: “To protect our marriage, I am willing to do this.” When we choose to be transparent and to keep each other informed, our spouse can rest easier, and that mutual peace of mind is the sturdiest fence of all.
q: In my work, ministry, or online life, is there any relationship with someone of the opposite sex where I need to redraw the lines?
Have I ever confided my dissatisfaction with my marriage to someone of the opposite sex? What did I really need at that time?
talk: For you, what ways of interacting with the opposite sex help you feel at ease? Which make you uneasy? Please be specific, and let’s not criticize each other.
What two or three boundaries could we set together to protect our marriage, ones we are both glad to keep rather than one of us imposing them on the other?
acts: Take the initiative to let your spouse know which people of the opposite sex you worked with today
Look over one message exchange that makes you uneasy, and draw a clear line if needed
Write down two boundaries for our home together with your spouse
lessons.noon: “How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God” — Lord, right now help me fear you and stay far from temptation.

lessons.title: Guarding Against Online Temptation and Pornography
lessons.theme: Make a covenant with your eyes and guard your home in a digital age

v: “I made a covenant with my eyes; how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?
I will be careful to live a blameless life. When will you come to me? I will walk within my house with a blameless heart.
I will set no vile thing before my eyes. I hate the deeds of faithless men. They will not cling to me.

lessons.still: Put your phone aside, screen down. Take a deep breath and tell the Lord, “Lord, my eyes, my time, and my heart all belong to you. Shine your light on everything I see today.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: With self on the throne we say, “I can control this myself,” and we fail again and again. Admitting “I can’t” is where victory begins. Not by gritting our teeth on our own strength, but by letting Jesus reign, following the Holy Spirit’s guidance, and gaining freedom step by step with the support of brothers and sisters.
lessons.jesus: In the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus told his disciples, “Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41). Jesus knew human weakness well. He didn’t dismiss it; he gave a way out: stay alert, and pray. In that hardest hour, he himself overcame through prayer.
lessons.pray: Holy and loving Lord, we make a covenant with our eyes and want to keep every vile thing out of our sight. Guard the doors of our home, our phones, and our hearts. If one of us is struggling right now, don’t let shame push them into the darkness; lead them by your grace toward the light and into freedom. Amen.
teach: Job said, “I made a covenant with my eyes; how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1). Job lived thousands of years ago, yet he already knew the eyes are the gateway to the heart, so he made a “covenant” with his eyes in advance. Today we have an extra window in front of us that is always open: our phones and the internet. Pornography is one tap away from entering our homes and our bedrooms, and it often comes knocking at our most tired, lonely, and stressed moments.

David said, “I will walk within my house with a blameless heart. I will set no vile thing before my eyes” (Psalm 101:2–3). “I will set no vile thing before my eyes” is an active decision, and it calls for practical safeguards: keep phones and computers in shared spaces at home; don’t take your phone to bed; install filtering software and let your spouse or a same-sex spiritual companion know the password; recognize the moments when you are most vulnerable, such as when you are hungry, angry, lonely, or tired, and plan a different way out ahead of time.

The harm of pornography is very real: it distorts how we see bodies and intimacy, turns people into objects to be consumed, and builds a wall of secrecy within a marriage. But remember: those who are trapped by it are not monsters; they are people who need rescuing. Shame makes people hide even more, and hiding tightens the chains; grace, though, opens a way out. If you are struggling with this right now, don’t fight alone. In the next lesson we will see together the way out that walks in the light.
q: Have I made a “covenant” with my eyes? At what times, in what moods, and on what devices am I most likely to look at what I shouldn’t?
What one practical change can I make now to “set no vile thing before my eyes”?
talk: Is there anything about how our home uses phones, computers, and the internet that we need to adjust together? For example, the bedroom, late nights, passwords, and filters.
If one day one of us became weak in this area, how would you want the other to tell you? And how would you respond?
acts: Tonight, charge your phone outside the bedroom
Check the filter settings on your home devices, and set them up together if needed
Write down the moments you are most vulnerable, and plan an alternative ahead of time
lessons.noon: “I will set no vile thing before my eyes” — Lord, right now guard my eyes and my heart.

lessons.title: Walking in the Light: Honesty and Accountability
lessons.theme: Grace gives those who fall a way out; honesty and accountability bring healing

v: But if we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son, cleanses us from all sin.
If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.

lessons.still: Sit quietly before the Lord. Whether your heart today is at peace, struggling, or wounded, you can tell him just as it is. He is light, and he is love; before him, you don’t need to hide.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life fears losing face more than anything, so it covers up; yet “He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper” (Proverbs 28:13). Humility is the key to renewal: when we let go of saving face and return to our rightful place before God, the blood of Jesus cleanses us. Life first, then relationship: when a life is healed, the marriage has a foundation to be rebuilt on.
lessons.jesus: A woman caught in adultery was dragged before Jesus, and the crowd wanted to stone her. Jesus said to her, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” (John 8:11). Jesus did not make light of sin, but he gave her grace and a way out first. He shows us that grace is not permission to keep sinning; it gives us the strength to start again.
lessons.pray: Lord of light and love, thank you that your blood cleanses us from all sin. Give us courage to walk in the light and stop hiding. Comfort and heal wounded hearts, and give those who have fallen the strength and a way to repent. Lead us to the right pastors and companions, so that through honesty and accountability we can rebuild this home together. Amen.
teach: John wrote, “if we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son, cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). Sin and temptation love the dark, the way mold grows best in damp, shadowy corners; open the window and let the sunlight in, and it loses its power. Walking in the light means no longer hiding our weakness, but letting God and people we trust see it.
