If you are already caught up in it, whether pornography, an inappropriate relationship, or some other secret, hear this good news: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins” (1 John 1:9). God is not waiting to punish you; he is waiting for you to come home. The first step out is to confess to God. The second is to come clean with your spouse in a fitting way, with a pastor or a mature spiritual mentor walking alongside you. The third is to seek professional marriage counseling or addiction counseling. This is not shameful; it is true courage.

James says, “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16). Healing takes time, and it takes community. For the spouse who has been hurt, the pain and anger are real, and you too need to be accompanied and cared for. Forgiveness is a process; it does not mean trust is restored immediately. Trust is rebuilt through time and action. If there is any threat, violence, or control in the relationship, safety always comes first: seek help from a pastor and professionals right away. God can rebuild broken walls, and he often does it through honesty and fellowship.
q: Is there a “dark corner” in my life that I have never dared to let God or anyone else see?
Is there a trustworthy, same-sex spiritual companion in my life who could be my accountability partner in this area?
talk: This week we have talked about the fences that guard our marriage. In which area would you most like us to strengthen things together? Whom could we invite to help us?
How can we let each other know, “Even if you fall, I am willing to walk with you into the light”? Tell me what you need.
acts: Tell God about one weakness you have kept hidden, and receive his forgiveness
Contact a same-sex spiritual companion and ask him or her to pray for you
If needed, write down the contact details of your church pastor or a counseling service
lessons.noon: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” — Lord, right now I come into your light; thank you for your forgiveness.

mem.t: Many waters can’t quench love, neither can floods drown it. If a man would give all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly scorned.

date.t: Retracing the Road of Our Love
s: Go back to a place that means something to you both: the restaurant of your first date, a park where you often walked, or look again at a photo from those early days.
Take turns saying: “Through every season we have walked together, one thing I am most grateful to you for is…”
Look back together over these nine weeks of the “Living” stage: time, money, and intimacy. Pick one good habit from each that you want to keep.
Hold hands and read Song of Songs 8:7, then bless each other: “May our love, in God, be something many waters can’t quench.”

lessons.title: Don’t Deprive One Another
lessons.theme: Intimacy in marriage is mutual giving, not one-sided taking

v: Let the husband give his wife the affection owed her, and likewise also the wife her husband.
The wife doesn’t have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise also the husband doesn’t have authority over his own body, but the wife does.

Don’t deprive one another, unless it is by consent for a season, that you may give yourselves to fasting and prayer, and may be together again, that Satan doesn’t tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

lessons.still: Be still and consider: “In our intimate relationship, do I think more often about ‘what I get’ or ‘what I give’?” Whatever the answer, bring it honestly before the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When self is on the throne, we read this passage and see only “You must not deprive me.” The self-emptied see “I don’t want to deprive you.” Pride turns Scripture into a weapon for making demands; humility turns it into a mirror for examining ourselves. Humility draws out humility, and then husband and wife both win.
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus “arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist” (John 13:4), and bent down to wash his disciples’ feet. He was the Lord, yet he did not demand to be served; he served first. Jesus shows us that love does not insist on its rights; it lays them down and seeks the other’s good first.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are Lord, yet you bent down to serve us. Remove from our hearts the self that only wants to take, so that in our marriage we give to each other and understand each other. Keep our intimacy blessed in respect and mutual consent. And protect everyone who is hurt or threatened in their marriage; lead them to safety and help. Amen.
teach: When Paul wrote to the church in Corinth, there were two extremes there: one indulged sexual desire freely, while the other believed abstinence was more spiritual, so that even husbands and wives deliberately kept their distance. Paul corrects both: “Let the husband give his wife the affection owed her, and likewise also the wife her husband” (1 Corinthians 7:3). In an age when men were ranked above women, Paul uses completely equal language: husband and wife have the same responsibility and the same respect toward each other.

Paul goes on: “The wife doesn’t have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise also the husband doesn’t have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (1 Corinthians 7:4). This does not give either side a right to “demand”; it calls both to lay down their own rights and give themselves to each other. Like two hands clasped together: not one grabbing the other, but both reaching out. That is why Paul says, “Don’t deprive one another,” and adds that even a time apart must be “by consent” (1 Corinthians 7:5). The key words are: one another, and consent.

So let us say it very clearly: any coercion, threat, or humiliation in the name of “submission” or “duty” is not biblical teaching; it is harm. Physical, verbal, sexual, and financial violence and control are not submission. If you are in such a situation, your safety comes first; please seek help from a pastor and professionals. On the other hand, life also has seasons of illness, recovery after childbirth, grief, and exhaustion, when intimacy calls for understanding and gentle conversation. Love does not keep score of who owes whom; it seeks the other’s good.
q: Have I ever taken “don’t deprive one another” to mean “you ought to satisfy me”? How has that thinking affected our relationship?
When it comes to intimacy, have I overlooked my spouse’s exhaustion, stress, or feelings?
talk: In the season of life we are in now (busyness, raising children, caring for parents, health issues, and so on), how do you think our intimacy needs us to understand each other and seek each other’s good?
What would make you feel treasured rather than pressured? Please be gentle and specific.
acts: Today, ask your spouse: “What has worn you out most lately? How can I help?”
Do one small act of service for your spouse without expecting anything back
Tell your spouse in one sentence: “I treasure you, not just need you.”
lessons.noon: “Let the husband give his wife the affection owed her, and likewise also the wife her husband” — Lord, right now help me think first of giving, not taking.

lessons.title: Do the First Works
lessons.theme: Rekindling love: remember, repent, and do again what we did at first

v: But I have this against you, that you left your first love.
Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works; or else I am coming to you swiftly, and will move your lamp stand out of its place, unless you repent.

lessons.still: Be still and remember the days when you first fell in love: the anticipation, the care you took, the things you said. Whisper to the Lord, “Lord, bring me back to my first love.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: With self on the throne, we wait for the other person to change first and reach out first. The self-emptied are willing to be the first to remember, the first to repent, the first to act. Change starts with me. When I first fix my eyes on Jesus and return to my first love for the Lord, his love wells up within me, and I find the strength to love my spouse again.
lessons.jesus: After Peter denied the Lord three times, Jesus prepared breakfast on the shore of the Sea of Galilee and then asked him, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15). Jesus took the initiative to restore Peter, rekindling his love on the very shore where he had first been called. He shows us that the renewal of love often begins with a loving invitation.
lessons.pray: Lord, giver of first love, thank you that you haven’t given up on us but gently call us to return. We admit our love has sometimes gone cold; forgive us, and help us remember, repent, and once again do the first works. Rekindle our love for you, and rekindle our love for each other. Amen.
teach: The risen Lord said to the church in Ephesus, “But I have this against you, that you left your first love” (Revelation 2:4). The Ephesian church was hardworking, patient, and discerning, yet it had lost its first love. These words were originally about the church’s love for the Lord, but they also act like a mirror, reflecting the state of many marriages: everything that should be done gets done, every responsibility is met, yet love seems to have gone cold.

The Lord didn’t only rebuke; he gave a clear way back: “Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works” (Revelation 2:5). Three verbs: remember, repent, do. To remember is to recall how we once saw each other and how much thought we put into each other. To repent is to admit what has cooled our love: perhaps busyness, resentment, or taking each other for granted. To do is to start doing again the things we did at the beginning.

Notice that the Lord says to “do” the first works, not to “wait” for the first feelings to come back. Feelings often follow actions, the way a match only lights once it is struck. A little note, a walk after dinner, a simple “You look lovely today”: each is a match struck anew. If your spouse doesn’t respond right away, don’t lose heart; love takes time and patience to warm up again. Rekindling love starts with me taking the first step.
q: What parts of the “first love” in our marriage have I let go of without even noticing?
What has made my love grow cold? Busyness, resentment, or taking my spouse for granted?
talk: Think back to when we were dating or newly married. What small thing made you feel especially loved? Could we bring it back?
This month, which of the “first works” would you most like us to do again together?
acts: Leave your spouse a little note: “I still love being with you.”
Do one small thing you often did while dating but have rarely done since
Give your spouse a sincere compliment
lessons.noon: “repent and do the first works” — Lord, right now bring me back to my first love.

lessons.title: Beautiful in Its Time
lessons.theme: Staying close in fitting ways through every season of life

v: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.
Even to old age I am he, and even to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear. Yes, I will carry, and will deliver.

lessons.still: Recall the seasons you have walked through from the day you met until now: newly married, moving house, job changes, illness, joys and losses. Quietly thank the Lord: “Lord, in every season, you have carried us.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When we shift from a temporary view to an eternal view, we no longer measure love only by physical condition, appearance, or passion. Earthly seasons change; God’s faithfulness does not. With our focus on Jesus, we can see the good things God has arranged in every season.
lessons.jesus: Even in his agony on the cross, Jesus saw his mother standing nearby and said to the disciple he loved, “Behold, your mother!” (John 19:27). In the hardest season of his life, Jesus still cared for the ones he loved. He shows us that true love, in every season, is willing to cherish and willing to carry.
lessons.pray: Lord of times and seasons, thank you for being with us in every season of our marriage. Help us not to cling to the past or resent the present, but to learn to draw close and cherish each other in the season we are in. Let our love become beautiful in its time, in every season. Amen.
teach: The Teacher says, “He has made everything beautiful in its time” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Marriage has its seasons too: the passion of the newlywed years, the chaos of raising children, the pressure of building a career, the weariness of midlife, the quiet of the empty nest, the mutual support of old age. In each season intimacy looks different, and God promises that every season can have a beauty of its own. What we need to learn is neither to cling to the past nor to resent the present, but to find, here and now, the good things God has prepared.

Some couples, because of illness, age, caring for family, or other reasons, find that physical intimacy has become rare or even impossible, and conclude in their hearts, “Our love is over.” But intimacy has never been just one form. In some seasons, intimacy is a look exchanged while caring for a family member late at night; in some, it is a hand held at a hospital bedside; in others, it is walking side by side every evening. The form changes; the connection can remain.

God says to his people, “Even to old age I am he, and even to gray hairs I will carry you” (Isaiah 46:4). God’s love doesn’t change with the seasons; he carries and holds us all the way. This becomes a model for how husband and wife treat each other: we don’t withdraw our love because our spouse has grown old, become ill, or is no longer as they used to be. In every season, ask honestly, “In this season, what makes you feel loved?” and keep bearing with each other and understanding each other.
q: Do I often long for “the old days” and overlook the good things God has prepared for us in this season?
In the season we are in now, what is one way I can help my spouse feel my closeness?
talk: What season of life do you think we are in right now? In this season, how do you most need me to be with you?
Think back to the hardest season we have walked through. What small things back then made you feel “we’re still in this together”?
acts: Ask your spouse: “In this season, what makes you feel most loved?”
Do one small act of closeness that suits this season, like rubbing their shoulders or walking side by side
Pray for a couple who is going through a hard season
lessons.noon: “Even to old age I am he, and even to gray hairs I will carry you” — Lord, right now help us hold each other up in every season.

lessons.title: Love Is Strong as Death
lessons.theme: Covenant love rooted in Christ cannot be quenched by many waters

v: Set me as a seal on your heart, as a seal on your arm; for love is strong as death. Jealousy is as cruel as Sheol. Its flashes are flashes of fire, a very flame of the LORD.
Many waters can’t quench love, neither can floods drown it. If a man would give all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly scorned.
For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers,
nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

lessons.still: Put your hand on your heart and feel it beating. Quietly hear the Lord say to you, “I have set you on my heart like a seal.” Let this love fill you, and then think of your spouse.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Human love runs dry; God’s love is the source. Love with self on the throne comes with conditions: I’ll love you if you treat me well. Self-emptied love enters the infinite, drawing on the boundless love of Christ. All the treasure on earth cannot buy love, but in Christ we have already received a love beyond price.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Not long after saying this, he went to the cross and proved these words with his life. Jesus’ love is strong as death; not even death could quench it, and three days later he rose again. This love is the source and the model of our married love.
lessons.pray: Lord whose love never ends, thank you for setting us on your heart like a seal; nothing can separate us from your love. Kindle our love with your flame, so that floods cannot quench it and suffering cannot drown it. Let our marriage be a witness to your everlasting love. Amen.
teach: The bride in the Song of Songs says, “Set me as a seal on your heart, as a seal on your arm” (Song of Songs 8:6). In ancient times a seal represented a person’s identity and authority; it was often worn on the chest or on the hand and never left them. What the bride longs for is a love that is public, exclusive, and never abandons her. Then she says, “love is strong as death” (Song of Songs 8:6). Death never lets go, and neither does true covenant love.

“Many waters can’t quench love, neither can floods drown it” (Song of Songs 8:7). In the Bible, mighty waters and floods often symbolize chaos and suffering. A marriage will meet many floods: financial pressure, illness, unemployment, misunderstanding, the loss of loved ones. Human passion can be doused, but the love God kindles is “a very flame of the LORD” (Song of Songs 8:6). Our love can withstand the floods not because we are so strong, but because it is joined to God.

Paul says that neither death nor life, neither things present nor things to come, “nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). This is the deepest root of our married love. When we are first held fast by this love, we find strength to hold on to each other even in the floods. Earthly marriage is a shadow of the love between Christ and the church; the faithfulness of husband and wife tells the world that God’s love never ends.
q: What “floods” has our marriage been through? At those times, what kept our love from being drowned?
Is my love more like human passion, or like a flame joined to God? Where do I need to draw love from?
talk: If you had to describe our love with one picture, what would you choose? Why?
Is there a “flood” pressing on you right now? How can I face it together with you?
acts: Tell your spouse: “Whatever floods we face, I will be with you.”
Write down a time when God’s grace carried you both through a “flood”
Pray specifically about the biggest pressure your spouse is facing right now
lessons.noon: “Many waters can’t quench love, neither can floods drown it” — Lord, right now let your love keep our love from ever going out.

lessons.title: Glorify God in Your Body
lessons.theme: Time, money, and body: do everything for the glory of God

v: Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own,
for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.
Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.

lessons.still: Look back over the past nine weeks: time, rest, dates, money, giving, intimacy, guarding. Quietly tell the Lord, “Lord, thank you for leading us all the way. Please keep changing the way we live.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change happens from the inside out in five layers: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. In this stage we have let God into the details of our daily living; when our daily living is offered to him, our relationships gain a new foundation. Let Jesus receive all the glory, so that even our family calendar, our budget, and our intimacy belong to him.
lessons.jesus: Before he was crucified, Jesus prayed to the Father, “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do” (John 17:4). Every day and every task of Jesus’ life was offered to the Father. He shows us that the most beautiful life is one in which ordinary days are lived as an offering to God.
lessons.pray: Lord, who bought us at a great price, thank you for leading us through these nine weeks, so that our time, money, and intimacy are turned more toward you. We are not our own; today we once again hand over our family calendar, our budget, our dinner table, and our bedroom to you. Help us, whether we eat or drink or whatever we do, to do all for your glory, and lead us into the next stage. Amen.
teach: Paul says, “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). “Body” here does not mean only our physical flesh; it means our whole self in everyday life: our time, our money, our eyes and hands, our intimacy. Jesus bought us back with his own life, so everything we have belongs to him. Worship doesn’t only happen in church on Sunday; it also happens at the dinner table on a Tuesday night, over the bills at the end of the month, and under the bedroom lamp.

These nine weeks have been the “Living” stage. We learned to number our days, to put down our phones and be present with each other, and to walk together in one heart. We learned that God is Lord over our money, to be content and of one mind, and to give generously. We learned about intimacy as God designed it, about fencing in our marriage, and about a love many waters can’t quench. These may look like very everyday topics, but in God’s eyes they are all places where we can glorify him. Change our lives, and our daily living will change.

Paul also says, “Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). The world tells us: your time is for yourself, your money is for spending on yourself, your body is for your own pleasure. The gospel tells us: all of it belongs to God, and living for God is where we find true freedom. In the next stage we enter the practice of “Relationships”: communication, conflict, submission, and boundaries. May we carry this way of living for God’s glory with us as we keep going.
q: Over these nine weeks, which lesson changed my mindset the most? What concrete change has it brought to my daily life?
Of the three areas (time, money, and body), which is hardest for me to “offer up” to God?
talk: During these nine weeks of the “Living” stage, what do you think has been our family’s biggest step forward? Please start by naming one change you have seen in me.
Next we will begin practicing communication and handling conflict. In which area would you most like us to grow together?
acts: Write down the most precious thing you gained in these nine weeks and share it with your spouse
Choose one good habit built during this stage and agree to keep it up
Pray together, entrusting the next stage of growth to God
lessons.noon: “whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” — Lord, right now I want my life today to glorify you.
